---

## California Gold Rush Era Locality Research Guide
**Place:** California, United States  
**Period:** 1848–1860 (Gold Rush and early statehood)  
**Focus:** Mining migration and settlement

---

### Jurisdictional Context

| Period | Status | Implication for Records |
|--------|--------|------------------------|
| Jan 1848 – Sept 1850 | U.S. military administration (no territorial government) | Minimal civil records; county system not yet established |
| Sept 9, 1850 | California admitted as the 31st state — **bypassed territorial status entirely** | County-level civil registration begins; federal census taken |
| 1850 onward | 27 original counties created; many more added through the decade | Records held at county level; search the county your ancestor was in |

California had no territorial phase, so there are no territorial-era record sets sitting between "Mexican California" and "U.S. state." The transition is abrupt: before September 1850, civil records are sparse; from late 1850 onward, county infrastructure begins generating records.

---

### ⚠️ Critical Quirks for This Period

1. **The 1850 federal census for California is partially destroyed.** Several county returns are missing entirely. Never assume your ancestor isn't findable — but do not expect complete coverage. The **1852 California State Census** is the essential substitute and filler; it is the only California state census ever taken and uniquely captures the Gold Rush population at its peak. Search it first.
2. **Civil registration of births and marriages was at county level from 1850; statewide registration did not begin until 1905.** For 1850s events, go to the county courthouse records or FamilySearch's county-level collections — there is no centralized state register for this period.
3. **The 1850s population was overwhelmingly transient and male.** Many miners left no local vital record at all. Mining claim registers, ship passenger manifests, land patents, and newspaper notices are often the only documentary trace of individuals.
4. **County boundaries changed frequently and rapidly in the 1850s.** A location recorded as one county in 1850 may have been carved into a new county by 1852 or 1855. Always verify which county held jurisdiction at the exact date of your event using a California county formation timeline before deciding where to search.
5. **The Great Registers (voter registration)** begin in 1866 — outside the 1850s window but invaluable for tracing men who stayed after the rush. FamilySearch collection 1923340 covers 1866–1910 with 1,345,678 indexed records. Treat it as the next-decade continuation of your search.

---

### Record Classes and Access

#### 1. Census Records — **Start here**

| Record | Date | Access | Notes |
|--------|------|--------|-------|
| **1850 U.S. Federal Census** | 1850 | Indexed + images (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | Partially destroyed for California — some counties missing |
| **1852 California State Census** | 1852 | **88% name-indexed; full-text searchable** (FamilySearch vol. 006601001, 522 images) | The single best snapshot of the Gold Rush population; names heads and household members |
| 1860 U.S. Federal Census | 1860 | Indexed + images | Complete; far better coverage than 1850 |
| **Mortality Schedules 1850, 1860** | 1850, 1860 | Indexed (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | Lists deaths in the 12 months preceding the census — critical for a population with high mortality from mining accidents and disease |

#### 2. Vital Records — County Level Only in the 1850s

| Record | FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Volume | Access |
|--------|------------------------|------------|--------|--------|
| **County Births** | [2017276](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) | 1850–1919 | 789,456 records / 394,728 images | Indexed + images |
| **County Marriages** | [1452832](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) | 1850–1952 | 567,890 records / 283,945 images | Indexed + images |

County death registers for this period are **not represented** in the collections returned — a coverage gap. Check individual county courthouses (county clerks) and the **California State Archives** in Sacramento for death records.

#### 3. Mining-Specific Records — Gold Rush Core Sources

| Record | Location / Access | Coverage | Access Level |
|--------|------------------|----------|--------------|
| **Mining Claim Registers** (San Francisco area) | FamilySearch vol. 006601002 (340 images) | 1849–1855 | **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image |
| **County Recorder Mining Claims** | County courthouses (physical or microfilm) | Varies by county | Physical/microfilm; check individual county archives |
| **Bureau of Land Management (BLM) General Land Office** | [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from 1850s | Indexed online — free |

Miners who filed claims with the county recorder left a paper trail with name, origin, and claim location. These records are held county-by-county; key mining counties include **El Dorado, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Nevada, Placer, and Sierra**. Contact those county archives directly.

#### 4. Arrival / Immigration Records — Tracing How They Got There

| Record | Location | Coverage | Access Level |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|
| **Ship Passenger Manifests (San Francisco)** | **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)) | 1849–1860s | Microfilm and digitized; also indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch |
| **Port Arrival Registers (Sacramento)** | FamilySearch vol. 006601003 (298 images) | 1849–1858 | **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable |
| **Overland Trail Diaries and Rosters** | Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley; California State Library | 1849–1855 | Physical manuscripts; some digitized and transcribed |

The vast majority of 49ers who came by sea arrived at **San Francisco**. NARA San Bruno holds the customs passenger lists. Those who came overland may appear in wagon company rosters and trail journals held at the Bancroft Library.

#### 5. Land Records

| Record | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **Federal Land Patents** | BLM GLO ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Free, name-indexed online |
| **County Deeds and Grants** | County recorders' offices | Physical or microfilm; some on FamilySearch |
| **Spanish/Mexican Land Grant Case Files** | National Archives (Washington, D.C.) and Bancroft Library | Physical; some finding aids online |

For families with pre-Gold Rush California roots, the **Mexican land grant records** and the U.S. Land Commission case files (1851–1855) that adjudicated those grants are a critical but often overlooked source.

#### 6. Court and Naturalization Records

Naturalizations before 1906 could be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. For 1850s California:
- **U.S. District Court records** → NARA San Bruno
- **County Superior Court records** → County courthouses; many counties also hold early naturalization papers
- Search FamilySearch's general U.S. naturalization holdings for any California-filed declarations

#### 7. Church Records

| Denomination / Record | Repository | Coverage | Notes |
|----------------------|-----------|----------|-------|
| **Catholic Mission Records** (baptisms, marriages, burials) | FamilySearch [1804372](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) | 1769–1850 | Pre-Gold Rush background; useful for Spanish/Mexican California families |
| **Catholic parish registers (1850s onward)** | Diocesan archives (Diocese of Sacramento, Archdiocese of San Francisco) | 1850s+ | Not broadly digitized; contact dioceses directly |
| **Protestant and other denominations** | Often held by the congregation or local historical societies; check the California State Library | 1850s onward | Coverage is sparse and uneven for the Gold Rush period |

#### 8. Newspapers

California had an active Gold Rush-era press. Newspapers carried **death notices, mining news, business advertisements, and letters to editors** — often the only surviving mention of a transient miner.

- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — full-text searchable, subscription
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection** ([cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu)) — free, full-text searchable; strong Gold Rush-era holdings including the *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849+)
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, [chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) — free; some California titles

#### 9. Military Records

Gold Rush migrants who served in the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) may appear in:
- **Mexican War service records and pension files** → NARA, Washington D.C.; also on Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) and Ancestry
- **California State Militia muster rolls (1850s)** → California State Archives, Sacramento

#### 10. Voter Registration — Great Registers (post-period, but essential for those who stayed)

FamilySearch collection [1923340](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340) — **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** — contains 1,345,678 indexed records. These registers required men to state their **birthplace, age, occupation, physical description, and naturalization status**, making them one of the richest identification sources for Gold Rush survivors who remained in California into the 1860s and beyond.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|-----------|--------------|--------|
| **FamilySearch.org** | State census 1852, county births/marriages, mission records, mining registers | Free online |
| **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** | Ship passenger lists, federal court records, naturalization files | In-person or online (Ancestry/Fold3 for many series) |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State government records, militia, some county records | In-person; limited online finding aids |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Manuscripts, Gold Rush diaries, local histories, newspaper archives | In-person; some digital |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Overland trail diaries, Mexican land grant files, Spanish-language records | In-person; some digital finding aids |
| **County Courthouses / County Archives** | Deeds, probate, court files, naturalization, marriage, birth | County by county — contact individually |
| **BLM General Land Office** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents | Free, online |

---

### Search Strategy Summary

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** (88% indexed on FamilySearch) — the single best Gold Rush snapshot.
2. **Check the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses**, noting the 1850 destruction gaps.
3. **Search ship passenger manifests** (NARA San Bruno / Ancestry / FamilySearch) if arrival was by sea via San Francisco.
4. **Identify the county** your ancestor mined or settled in, then go to that county's recorder and courthouse records for deeds, claims, and court files. County boundaries shifted rapidly — verify the 1850s jurisdiction.
5. **Browse mining claim registers** on FamilySearch (image-by-image; not indexed) if the county is known.
6. **Search the California Digital Newspaper Collection** for death notices and mentions.
7. **Extend into the Great Registers (1866+)** for men who stayed in California after the rush.
8. **Check federal land patents** at BLM GLO for those who transitioned from mining to farming or ranching.

---

**Note on volume search coverage:** FamilySearch returned 14 digitized volumes for California in this period; only the first page (3 volumes) was detailed above. Additional volumes may cover other counties or record types. If you need a fuller picture of a specific county's digitized holdings, that's worth a targeted follow-up search by county.

## Locality Research Guide: New York City, Colonial Period (1700–1783)

### Jurisdictional Context

New York City in the 1700s was essentially coextensive with **Manhattan Island / New York County**, the seat of New York Province under British colonial rule. The city had been Dutch New Amsterdam (1626–1664) before the English seized it and renamed it. That Dutch legacy persists deep into the 1700s: many families continued using Dutch naming conventions and Dutch-language records long after the English takeover. The Province's administrative center was the city itself, so many provincial-level records (wills, court files, land patents) were created and held there.

**Critical jurisdictional note:** There was **no statewide civil vital registration** during this period. Church registers are the primary — often the only — source for births, marriages, and deaths. New York did not become a state until 1788, after the colonial period ends; records before that date are colonial provincial records, not state records.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. Church Records ⭐ *Primary vital source for this period*

The sole source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in colonial NYC. Three denominations dominate:

| Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Dutch Reformed** | Oldest continuous series, beginning 1639. Services and records in Dutch. |
| **Anglican (Trinity Church)** | Founded 1697; registers from that year. Held at Trinity Church Archives, Manhattan. |
| **Presbyterian** | Early establishment; records at denominational archives. |

**FamilySearch digitized:**
- **Collection: "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"** (id: 1469062) — covers the target period. [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)
- **Digitized volume: Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City 1700–1776** (image group 007733180, 211 images) — ⚠️ **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; records are in Dutch.** Must be browsed image by image; researcher must be able to read Dutch or use a translator.

**Key repository:** New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial church record collections.

📎 Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

#### 2. Probate Records (Wills & Estate Files)

Colonial-era wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** — a *provincial-level* court, not a county court. This is a key quirk: do not look for these only at the county level.

- The New-York Historical Society published the **Abstracts of Wills** series, which indexes colonial-era wills. This is a standard finding aid for this period.
- **FamilySearch collection: "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971"** (id: 1542780, ~987,654 records) covers the target period. [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)

📎 Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

---

#### 3. Land Records

Colonial land grants, patents, and conveyances are among the richest sources for placing a family in a specific location and time.

- **FamilySearch collection: "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975"** (id: 2078654, ~1,567,890 records) — covers the full colonial period. [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives (Albany) — the main repository for provincial land patents and administrative records.

📎 Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

#### 4. Court Records

The **Mayor's Court** was the principal civil court in colonial New York City. Its records can name parties, witnesses, and kin, and include some naturalization proceedings.

- Records are held in the **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives.
- The New-York Historical Society and NYGBS also hold transcripts and abstracts of colonial court records.

📎 Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

#### 5. Tax Records

Colonial tax assessment lists survive for some years and individual wards of the city. These can document a family's presence and approximate economic status.

- **FamilySearch collection: "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804"** (id: 1678432) — only the very tail end overlaps the colonial period (1799–1800). [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) For earlier colonial tax lists, consult the New York State Archives directly.

📎 Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

---

#### 6. Militia Rolls

Colonial New York Province maintained **militia rolls** listing men of military age — useful for identifying male residents in a household during years when no other record survives.

- Held at the New York State Archives; some transcribed lists appear in published genealogical society volumes.

📎 Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

---

#### 7. Newspapers

The **New York Gazette** (established 1725, the province's first newspaper) published notices of deaths, marriages, property sales, runaway servants, and merchant activities. These can corroborate or supplement church and court records.

- Available on microfilm and through digitized newspaper archives (e.g., Newspapers.com, Readex/America's Historical Newspapers).

---

#### 8. Census Records

⚠️ **No U.S. Federal Census exists for the colonial period** — the first federal census was 1790, after the Revolution. For the 1700s, the nearest equivalents are scattered provincial enumerations and tax lists. The 1790 census (available on FamilySearch and Ancestry) is a useful post-colonial anchor for families still in the city.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** (Albany, NY) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, land patents, court records, militia rolls | In-person and some digitized finding aids online |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Colonial NYC church abstracts, vital record transcripts, published volumes | Membership; some records on Ancestry.com |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Abstracts of Wills series, colonial collections | In-person; library membership |
| **Trinity Church Archives** (Manhattan) | Anglican registers from 1697 | Contact archives directly |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Church records, land records, probate records (collections listed above) | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Post-1790 federal records; some colonial-era Revolutionary War records | In-person and online via Fold3 |

---

### Key Quirks for This Period

1. **No civil vital registration in the 1700s.** Church registers are the only systematic source for births, marriages, and deaths. Identify the family's denomination first.
2. **Dutch-language records persist well into the 1700s.** The Dutch Reformed Church records (including the digitized 1700–1776 volume on FamilySearch) are in Dutch and must be browsed image by image — they are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable.
3. **Wills were proved at the provincial (Prerogative Court) level,** not the county level. Search the NYHS Abstracts of Wills series and the FamilySearch probate collection, not only county-level records.
4. **"New York City" in the 1700s = Manhattan/New York County only.** The five-borough city is a creation of 1898. Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, and the Bronx were separate jurisdictions with their own records during the colonial period.
5. **The first U.S. Census is 1790** — after the colonial period. For the 1700s, use tax lists and militia rolls as substitutes for census-type residence evidence.
6. **Dutch naming conventions** (patronymics, recycled given names across generations) were still common in NYC Dutch families throughout the 1700s. Expect a father named Pieter to have sons and grandsons named Pieter, and patronymic surnames (e.g., "Pietersen" = son of Pieter) that may vary across records.

---

### Recommended Starting Strategy

1. **Identify denomination** → locate the relevant church register series.
2. **Search FamilySearch** collections 1469062 (church), 2078654 (land), and 1542780 (probate) for the family surname.
3. **Browse the Dutch Reformed Church register volume** (image group 007733180) if the family is of Dutch descent — remember it's Dutch-language and browse-only.
4. **Check the NYHS Abstracts of Wills** for any male ancestor who died in New York Province.
5. **Contact NYGBS and the New-York Historical Society** for manuscript collections not yet digitized.
6. **Search colonial tax lists and militia rolls** at the New York State Archives to document presence between church record appearances.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States — Revolutionary War Period (1775–1783)
**Focus: Military Service and Wartime Activities**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia operated as the **Commonwealth of Virginia** throughout the war, becoming a formal U.S. state in 1788. The **county** was the foundational administrative unit for virtually all record-keeping — courts, tax lists, land deeds, and church parishes all functioned at the county level. There were roughly 60–80 counties in existence across the war years; boundaries shifted as the frontier expanded, so knowing which county your ancestor lived in (and whether that county had been carved from a larger parent) is essential before searching.

> **Critical gap:** The **1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. This means there is no standard first-census snapshot for Virginia families. The **1782–1787 county personal property and land tax lists** are the primary substitute and fall almost perfectly at the close of the war.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Virginia Military Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))*

---

## Military Records — Tier 1 (Start Here)

Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Virginia Military Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))*

### 1. Continental Army Service Records and Muster Rolls
- **What they contain:** Compiled service records documenting enlistments, discharges, pay, and muster rolls listing soldiers present for duty
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), **Record Group 93**
- **How to access:** [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) — in person, or order copies through NARA's online request system; also digitized on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com))
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed + images on Fold3; browse-only images for some series

### 2. Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files
- **What they contain:** Post-war applications filed by veterans and their widows — often the richest biographical source, including ages, birthplaces, unit details, names of family members, and witness depositions
- **Where held:** NARA, **Record Group 15**
- **How to access:** Digitized on **Fold3**; many are also transcribed and indexed on **Ancestry.com**
- **Timing note:** Most files were created after 1818 (the first federal pension act covering service) or after 1832 — they are post-period documents but contain detailed wartime information
- **Digitization level:** Large portion indexed + images on Fold3 and Ancestry

### 3. Virginia Militia Records
- **What they contain:** Muster rolls, pay records, and rosters for Virginia state militia troops — distinct from Continental Line soldiers, who appear in NARA RG 93
- **Where held:** **Library of Virginia**, Richmond, VA ([lva.virginia.gov](https://lva.virginia.gov))
- **Critical quirk:** Many Virginia men served only in the state militia and do **not** appear in federal NARA records. If your ancestor isn't in NARA RG 93, check the Library of Virginia before concluding he did not serve.
- **Digitization level:** Partially digitized; some browse-only microfilm; physical research or written requests may be needed

### 4. Virginia State Navy Records
- **What they contain:** Service records for Virginia's wartime state navy
- **Access:** Published and compiled — consult the FamilySearch Wiki page at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) for specific publication citations

---

## Bounty Land Records — Post-War Trail Back to Service

Virginia granted **bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio** to its Revolutionary War veterans. If a veteran is hard to trace through service records, his land warrant or survey may be the documentary thread that proves service.

- **Warrant and survey records:** Virginia State Library (now the Library of Virginia), Richmond
- **What they connect:** Veteran name → land claim → confirmation of military service
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Virginia Military Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))*

---

| Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 | 1775–1783 | [collection/1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) |
| Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 | 1680–1929 | [collection/1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) |
| Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 | 1600–1900 | [collection/1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) |
| Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 | 1782–1850 | [collection/1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) |

> **Note:** The tool returned record counts for these collections but the values appeared to be placeholder figures. Verify current counts and indexing status directly on FamilySearch before drawing conclusions about coverage.

---

## Tax Lists — The Census Substitute (Critically Important)

Because no 1790 Virginia census survives, the **1782–1787 county personal property and land tax lists** are your primary tool for placing a household in a specific county at the close of the war. These lists:
- Name heads of household and taxable male members (often 16+)
- Record slaveholding, livestock, and land — evidence of economic standing
- Are available through FamilySearch (**Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850**, collection above) and the Library of Virginia

---

## County Court Records — Wartime Documents

County order books, minute books, and deed books from 1775–1783 can contain:
- **Oaths of loyalty** to Virginia (required during the war; refusal marked a Loyalist)
- **Claims for militia service** and supply requisitions
- **Land grants and deeds** recording wartime transactions
- **Guardianship and orphan records** when soldiers died leaving minor children
- **Wills and inventories** of men who died during service

**Where held:** County courthouses (originals); Library of Virginia (microfilm and some digital); FamilySearch **Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920**

---

## Church Records

Virginia's established church before the Revolution was **Anglican (Church of England)**, disestablished during the war and succeeded by the Episcopal Church. Parish vestry books and registers recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials and are sometimes the only record of family events in this period. FamilySearch holds **Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929** (overlaps the war years). Dissenting congregations — Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist — also kept registers; their records are often held by denominational archives or the Library of Virginia.

---

## Land Records

- **Deeds and patents:** County courthouse deed books (Library of Virginia; some on FamilySearch via Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records)
- **Wartime grants:** Virginia issued land grants to soldiers and settlers; colonial and early state land grants are indexed at the Library of Virginia
- **Virginia Military District of Ohio:** Separate bounty land series, described above under Post-War Bounty Lands

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Continental service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) | In person / mail / Fold3 |
| **Library of Virginia** (lva.virginia.gov) | State militia records, county records, bounty land warrants | In person / online catalog / written requests |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Digitized NARA pension files, service records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | Compiled pension/military databases, some county records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Virginia wartime newspapers (casualty notices, bounty ads) | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery memorials, including veterans' markers | Free |

---

## Research Quirks to Know Before You Search

1. **No 1790 Virginia census** — go straight to the 1782–1787 county tax lists.
2. **State militia ≠ NARA** — militia-only soldiers appear at the Library of Virginia, not in federal records. Always check both.
3. **Pension files are post-war but rich** — filed mostly 1818–1840s, they often contain the most detailed narrative of a man's wartime life.
4. **Virginia Military District of Ohio** — if service records are missing, the Ohio bounty land warrant may be the only surviving proof of service.
5. **FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for Virginia** returned only generic content in this survey — consult the Virginia Military Records article directly at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) for additional compiled sources, published rosters, and DAR/SAR lineage tools.
6. **Loyalist families** — if an ancestor refused an oath of loyalty, look for court order books recording the refusal, and check British Loyalist claims records at Library and Archives Canada or The National Archives (UK).
7. **County boundary changes** — if a county was carved from a parent during or after the war, earlier records will be in the parent county's books. Verify your county's formation date before searching.

## A Suggested Search Order

1. **NARA RG 93** (via Fold3) — Continental service record
2. **NARA RG 15** (via Fold3/Ancestry) — pension file
3. **Library of Virginia** — Virginia militia records if not found in step 1
4. **FamilySearch: Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850** — place the family in a county
5. **FamilySearch: Virginia, County Court Records** — oaths, claims, deeds, wills
6. **Library of Virginia bounty land warrants** — confirm service via Ohio land claim
7. **Church records and land deeds** — fill in family structure around the soldier

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

New Orleans sits in **Orleans Parish** — Louisiana uses *parishes* rather than counties, a legacy of its French and Spanish Catholic administrative tradition. The early 1800s mark a dramatic jurisdictional transition through three sovereignties:

| Period | Sovereignty | Legal tradition |
|---|---|---|
| 1800–1803 | French colonial (returned under Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800) | Napoleonic Code |
| 1803 | Louisiana Purchase — becomes U.S. territory | Civil law retained |
| 1804–1812 | Territory of Orleans | Hybrid civil / U.S. territorial |
| 1812–present | State of Louisiana | Napoleonic Code (civil law) |

**Why this matters for research:** Louisiana did not adopt English common law. It retained the **Napoleonic Code**, which creates a fundamentally different record landscape: notarial acts replace deed books and many court filings; "successions" replace probate; "tutorships" replace guardianship. A researcher expecting common-law records will miss the most important sources.

- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish seat of Orleans Parish)
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools; historically the city grew from roughly 8,000 at the Louisiana Purchase (1803) to over 100,000 by 1840, driven by the cotton and sugar trades, the internal slave trade, and successive waves of immigration
- **Economy:** Major port city — the second-largest US port by the 1840s. Cotton, sugar, slave trading, and Mississippi River/steamboat commerce generated enormous volumes of legal and commercial paperwork
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, Anglo-Americans, free people of color (*gens de couleur libres* — one of the largest free Black communities in antebellum America), enslaved Africans and African Americans, German immigrants, Irish immigrants, and ~9,000 Saint-Domingue (Haitian) refugees who arrived in 1809 via Cuba
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral, est. 1718; additional parishes added through the 1820s–1840s); Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) established after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Fires of 1788 and 1794 (colonial-record losses); Louisiana Purchase 1803; Territory of Orleans 1804; Battle of New Orleans January 8, 1815; statehood 1812; recurring yellow fever epidemics (major outbreaks 1817–1820, 1832–33, 1837, 1847)

## Boundary changes

- Orleans Parish was established by the territorial government in 1807, encompassing the city of New Orleans and surrounding lands. It has remained the jurisdiction for the city of New Orleans since.
- For events **before 1803**, authority rested with the **Spanish colonial government** (Cabildo) from 1763–1803, and with the **French colonial government** before 1763. Records from those periods do not belong to any U.S. jurisdictional chain — they sit in church archives, the New Orleans Notarial Archives, and (for Spanish administrative records) the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain.
- The city limits of New Orleans expanded throughout the period, absorbing the neighboring municipalities of Lafayette, Jefferson City, Algiers, and others — some lying in adjacent Jefferson Parish. If an ancestor lived in what is now New Orleans but outside the original city limits, check Jefferson Parish records as well.

---

## ⚠️ Disaster record losses and what survived

This is the central challenge of New Orleans research and the specific question you asked. Here is a full account by disaster and what substitute sources compensate for each loss.

### The Great Fire of Good Friday, 1788
Destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter and consumed many civil records from the **French colonial period (1718–1763)**.

**What survived:**
- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers:** The Catholic Church maintained its registers separately from civil administration. Baptisms, marriages, and burials survive from **1731** (with gaps for the fire year itself), because the church stored its records independently. These are the single most important surviving source for vital events. ([FamilySearch Wiki: New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (NONAR) stores records dating to **1734** in a dedicated archive. These survived because notarial acts were kept in a separate, purpose-built repository. NONAR holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts. ([FamilySearch Wiki: New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))
- **Spanish colonial Cabildo records:** The Cabildo (the Spanish colonial governing body) maintained its own administrative records, now held at the **Louisiana State Museum / The Cabildo** in New Orleans.

### The Second Great Fire, 1794
Destroyed additional buildings. Spanish colonial authorities undertook reconstruction efforts and in some cases recreated or reconstructed records.

**What survived / substitutes:**
- Same repositories as above: St. Louis Cathedral registers, NONAR notarial acts, Cabildo records
- Some records reconstructed by Spanish authorities after 1794
- Copies of certain Louisiana records were held in Spain at the **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)** — a duplicate administrative chain outside Louisiana entirely, unaffected by local fires

### Ongoing flood, hurricane, and climate damage (1800–1850)
New Orleans's low-lying terrain and recurring storms caused scattered water damage to archival holdings throughout the period. Individual record volumes may have gaps, water staining, or missing pages as a result. No single catastrophic flood-related loss comparable to the fires occurred in this period, but climate damage is pervasive in surviving collections.

**Substitute strategy:** When a register volume has a gap or damage, cross-reference the parallel church series (e.g., if a burial register is damaged, check baptism records for the same individual's godparents, or notarial succession records for the estate).

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no comprehensive statewide civil registration in Louisiana for 1800–1850. The **Louisiana Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964** (FamilySearch collection 1543892) indicates that death records at some level begin in **1819**. The **Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957** collection (1798054) shows formal parish-level marriage registration from **1837**. For births: no civil birth registration system operated in New Orleans during the early 1800s.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) for civil records; FamilySearch for digitized collections
- **Gaps:** No civil birth registration before approximately the 1840s–1850s; marriage civil registration incomplete before 1837; death registration present from 1819 but coverage uneven
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731) are the effective substitute for all civil vital records in 1800–1837

### Church records ⭐ *(Most important source for the entire 1800–1850 period)*

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic dominant. St. Louis Cathedral (Cathedral-Basilica of Saint Louis, King of France) is the oldest continuously used Catholic cathedral in the United States, with sacramental records from 1731. Separate registers were maintained for free people of color and enslaved persons. Additional Catholic parishes formed as the city expanded (St. Patrick's 1833, for Irish immigrants; others through the 1840s).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Separate registers for enslaved persons and free people of color — a critical source for researching those communities.
- **Language:** French (French colonial period through the Creole tradition, often persisting into the 1840s); Spanish (Spanish colonial period records, 1763–1803); English increasingly after 1803 but Catholic registers often stayed in French/Spanish for decades.
- **Where held:**
  - **FamilySearch Collection 1612905 — Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925:** Indexed + images; ~987,654 records; covers the full target period. Search at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)
  - **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** (physical): Original registers and additional records not fully captured online

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The **first federal census for New Orleans is 1810** — Louisiana was not yet US territory when the 1800 census was taken. Available censuses for the target period: **1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850**. All are indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Pre-US enumerations:** Spanish colonial *padrones* (population listings) from 1763–1803 survive in the Louisiana State Archives and Archivo General de Indias. These are the only population-level records for the Spanish period equivalent to a census.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry; fully name-searchable.

### Probate and succession records ⭐

- **Louisiana terminology:** Inheritance proceedings are called **successions** (not probate). The Civil District Court for Orleans Parish handled both testate ("testamentary succession") and intestate ("intestate succession") estates. **Tutorships** (guardianship for minors) are separate dockets and equally valuable for establishing parent–child relationships. **Interdictions** (declared mental incapacity) are another civil-law record type with no direct common-law equivalent.
- **FamilySearch Collection 2078341 — Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984:** Indexed + images; ~456,789 records; covers 1800–1850. Search at [familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)
- **Estate inventories:** Under the Louisiana civil law system, succession inventories are exceptionally detailed — listing every piece of property (furniture, tools, clothing, livestock, and before abolition, enslaved individuals by name with valuations). These are among the most genealogically rich records in the state.
- **Where held:** Civil District Court for Orleans Parish (originals); Louisiana State Archives (territorial-era records); FamilySearch (digitized)

### Notarial records ⭐ *(Unique to Louisiana — the premier substitute for missing records of every type)*

- **Why essential:** In Louisiana's civil law system, the notary (*notaire*) authenticated virtually all significant legal acts: property sales, mortgages, marriage contracts, wills (testaments), apprenticeships, manumissions, slave sales, commercial partnerships, and more. A notarial act touching your ancestor may reveal birth dates, places of origin, family relationships, occupations, and residence addresses — in a single document.
- **NONAR:** The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts from **1734**, organized by notary name and date. Physical address: 1 Poydras Street, New Orleans. Partial online index at [nolanotarialarchives.org](http://www.nolanotarialarchives.org). This is the single most important physical repository for 1800–1850 research.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** **1 volume** — Orleans notarial acts 1803–1820 (167 images, **0% name-indexed, NOT fulltext searchable — must be browsed image by image**, in French and English). Image group 004990115. This represents a tiny fraction of NONAR's holdings; plan an in-person or correspondence visit for records beyond this range.
- **Language:** French and Spanish through the 1810s–1820s; increasingly English after 1815, but many notaries continued in French through the 1840s.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Louisiana is a **state-land state** for pre-US grants. French and Spanish colonial grants used the **French long-lot (arpent) system** — narrow strips perpendicular to rivers, not the federal township-range grid. After 1803, federal grants used rectangular survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pre-1803 grants: **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge) and **Louisiana State Archives**; Spanish originals at AGI (Seville). Post-1803 federal grants: **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov — free and searchable online).
- **Property transfers 1800–1850:** Recorded as notarial acts at NONAR — not in common-law deed books. The FamilySearch digitized notarial volume (1803–1820, browse-only) is the only online option; all other transfers require NONAR.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The **Battle of New Orleans, January 8, 1815** (War of 1812) is the dominant military event of the period. Louisiana territorial militia and the **Battalion of Free Men of Color** — an organized free Black military unit dating to the Spanish colonial period — participated alongside Jackson's forces. Service records and pension files are at NARA and Fold3.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, muster rolls, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com), subscription); NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) for federal records; Louisiana State Archives for territorial militia records

### Cemetery records

- **Context:** Yellow fever epidemics caused enormous mortality throughout the period. New Orleans's above-ground burial (driven by the high water table) in walled tomb cities creates a distinctive physical record.
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823). Protestant cemeteries (Lafayette Cemetery No. 1, est. 1833; Girod Street Cemetery, est. 1822) serve the Anglo-American community.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has listings for many New Orleans cemeteries, but coverage for 1800–1850 burials is uneven and often lacks images or full dates.
- **Physical records:** St. Louis Cathedral burial registers (part of FamilySearch collection 1612905); sexton records for individual cemeteries held at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records

- **Key titles:**
  - *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (French-language, est. 1794)
  - *Louisiana Gazette* (est. 1804 — first American newspaper in New Orleans)
  - *New Orleans Bee / L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans* (bilingual French–English, est. 1827)
  - *Daily Picayune* (est. 1837)
- **Genealogical value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale notices, sheriff's sale notices (land/property auctions for debt), and — critically for African American research — **runaway slave advertisements**, which name individuals and sometimes describe physical features, family connections, and origins.
- **Where held:**
  - Newspapers.com (subscription): Some New Orleans papers
  - Chronicling America ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov), free): Library of Congress historic newspapers — check Louisiana coverage
  - New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division: Microfilm holdings of many titles
  - Historic New Orleans Collection (THNOC): Extensive local newspaper holdings

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Port of New Orleans:** One of the major US ports of entry in the early 1800s. German and Irish immigration surged in the 1820s–1840s; significant arrivals also from France, Spain, and the Caribbean.
- **1809 Saint-Domingue influx:** Approximately 9,000 refugees arrived in 1809 from Cuba (originally fleeing the Haitian Revolution) — including a large contingent of free people of color. This is a specific, well-documented migration event; researchers with ancestors in this cohort should search New Orleans passenger lists and church records from 1809–1815.
- **Passenger lists:** Available from NARA for the port of New Orleans; Ancestry has indexed many (search "New Orleans Passenger Lists" or "New Orleans Ship Manifests"). Coverage improves from the 1820s; pre-1820 lists are sparser.
- **Naturalization:** Louisiana's civil law tradition means naturalization records may appear in district court files or even notarial acts — not only in federal court filings. NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) holds federal naturalization records pre-1906.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax (real and personal property), poll tax — assessed at the parish level
- **Substitute value:** For years between federal censuses (e.g., 1815–1819, 1821–1829, 1831–1839, 1841–1849), Orleans Parish tax assessment rolls can confirm an ancestor's presence and sometimes list property descriptions or occupants.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); Orleans Parish Assessor's Office. Limited digitization — primarily physical access only.

### Other record types

**Records of enslaved persons and free people of color:**
- **Notarial acts** at NONAR document slave sales, manumissions, and freedom paper registrations — often the only record naming enslaved individuals.
- **St. Louis Cathedral** maintained separate baptismal, marriage, and burial registers for enslaved persons and free people of color — included in FamilySearch collection 1612905.
- **Runaway slave advertisements** in New Orleans newspapers name individuals with physical descriptions and sometimes family or origin information.
- **Succession inventories** list enslaved individuals by name with valuations.

**City directories:**
- New Orleans directories appear from the early 1800s. They place individuals at specific addresses in years between censuses.
- Historic New Orleans Collection (THNOC) and New Orleans Public Library hold early directories. Some digitized on Ancestry (search "New Orleans, Louisiana City Directories").

## Records NOT online

- **Notarial acts (the overwhelming majority):** NONAR holds 30+ million pages; FamilySearch has digitized only 167 images (1 volume, 1803–1820, browse-only). Everything else requires in-person or correspondence access to NONAR.
- **City tax assessment rolls:** Largely physical at Louisiana State Archives and Orleans Parish Assessor's Office.
- **Early city directories (pre-1840s):** Primarily at THNOC and New Orleans Public Library.
- **Territorial-era court records (1804–1812):** Partially physical at Louisiana State Archives; limited digitization.
- **Spanish colonial records at AGI (Seville):** Some digitized via PARES; most require in-person access or ordering.
- **Cemetery sexton records:** Physical at Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and individual cemetery offices.
- **Civil birth records (pre-1840s–1850s):** No systematic civil birth registration existed; church sacramental registers (partly online in collection 1612905) are the only systematically kept record.

## Known record losses

| Loss | Date | What was destroyed | Best substitutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Fire of Good Friday | 1788 | ~856 buildings in the French Quarter; French colonial-era civil records | St. Louis Cathedral registers (from 1731, with gaps); NONAR notarial acts (from 1734); Cabildo records at Louisiana State Museum |
| Second Great Fire | 1794 | Additional buildings and records | Same as above; some reconstructed by Spanish authorities; AGI (Seville) holds Spanish administrative duplicates unaffected by local fires |
| Flood and hurricane damage (ongoing) | Throughout 1800–1850 | Scattered damage across parish archives, individual volumes | Cross-reference parallel church registers; notarial succession records; newspaper notices |
| Yellow fever epidemic mortality outpacing record-keeping | 1817–1820, 1830s, 1847 | Burial registers may be incomplete during peak epidemic years | Multiple independent church registers; notarial succession records for estates; newspaper death notices |

## Research tips

1. **Start with church records, not civil registration.** Civil registration was absent for births and incomplete for marriages through most of 1800–1850. FamilySearch collection 1612905 (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) is indexed and imaged — start here. ([FamilySearch Wiki: New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

2. **Notarial records are Louisiana's most distinctive and most overlooked source.** If your ancestor bought property, inherited, married, freed an enslaved person, or entered any legal agreement, a notarial act exists. NONAR's 30+ million pages are the target; the 1 FamilySearch volume (browse-only, 1803–1820) is only a preview. Plan an in-person visit or written inquiry to NONAR.

3. **Records through the 1820s–1830s are often in French or Spanish.** Catholic sacramental registers, notarial acts, and many civil records require reading French or Spanish. The indexed FamilySearch collections provide English-language summaries as finding aids; always verify against the original image.

4. **Use successions, not just "wills."** Louisiana succession inventories are exceptionally detailed under civil law — listing all property and (before 1865) enslaved individuals by name. Search FamilySearch collection 2078341. Look for both testate (testamentary) and intestate filings, plus tutorship records for minor children.

5. **The 1810 census is the first federal census for New Orleans.** There is no 1800 federal census for Louisiana. For 1800–1809, use Spanish colonial padrones (Louisiana State Archives, AGI) and St. Louis Cathedral registers.

6. **For Spanish colonial ancestors (events 1763–1803), check AGI in Seville.** The Archivo General de Indias holds Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana. Some are digitized at [pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es); others require in-person access. Louisiana State Archives holds microfilm transcripts of some AGI holdings.

7. **For enslaved and free Black ancestors, the notarial archives and separate sacramental registers are essential.** St. Louis Cathedral's separate registers for enslaved persons and free people of color are in collection 1612905. Manumissions, freedom paper registrations, and slave sale records are in NONAR notarial acts. The 1809 Saint-Domingue refugee cohort is a traceable population group with its own paper trail.

8. **Search newspapers for legal and vital notices.** Sheriff's sales, estate notices, marriage announcements, and runaway slave advertisements all appeared in New Orleans papers. The *Louisiana Gazette* (from 1804) and *New Orleans Bee* (from 1827) are key titles. Use Newspapers.com, Chronicling America, and the New Orleans Public Library's microfilm holdings.

9. **Battle of New Orleans records are a significant source.** The January 8, 1815 engagement generated extensive military records, including for the Free Men of Color battalion. Fold3 and NARA hold service records. These can confirm presence, physical description, and sometimes family status.

10. **Check Jefferson Parish for ancestors at the city's edges.** The city limits of New Orleans expanded across the period, and neighboring Jefferson Parish held jurisdiction over areas now part of the city. If an ancestor is missing from Orleans Parish records, check Jefferson Parish records.

## Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Immigrant Arrivals, 1840s

**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period of focus:** 1840–1850
**Jurisdictional anchor:** Boston has been an incorporated city since 1822; it is the county seat of Suffolk County and the Massachusetts state capital.

---

### Historical Context

Boston was one of five major U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s. Immigration surged dramatically during the Irish Great Famine (1845–1852); by 1850, more than a quarter of Boston's population was Irish-born. Immigrants settled principally in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods. Massachusetts statewide vital registration began in **1841**, though town clerks had been ordered to record births, marriages, and deaths since **1639** — so civil vital records exist throughout the 1840s at both the town and state level.

---

### 1. Passenger / Arrival Lists ⭐ Primary source

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) — name-indexed |
| **Digitized volume** | Image group 003345210 — 389 images, Port of Boston, 1840–1850 |
| **Indexing level** | 3% name-indexed; **full-text searchable** — treat as full-text/browse-only, not a standard name search |
| **Also indexed on** | Ancestry.com |
| **Originals** | NARA Record Group 36, held at the **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA** |

**⚠ Important limitation:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Immigration — Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)), 1840s customs passenger lists typically record only **name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin** — not the specific county, parish, or townland. Finding an exact place of origin almost always requires corroborating sources.

**⚠ Coverage note:** The volume search returned **only 1 digitized volume** (003345210) for the 1840–1850 Boston window. The broader passenger list collection (id: 1784312) reports 617,283 images, so this is likely a partial digitization picture. Check FamilySearch for additional volumes and consult NARA Waltham for any gaps.

---

### 2. Naturalization Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — name-indexed |
| **Originals** | NARA (archives.gov); Massachusetts State Archives |

Before 1906, an immigrant could naturalize in **any willing court** — federal district, state superior, or local municipal. Boston-area naturalizations may therefore appear across multiple court jurisdictions. Search all three levels for Suffolk County. Early 1840s naturalizations may contain more detail than the passenger list that preceded them.

---

### 3. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths in Massachusetts)

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — name-indexed |
| **Statewide registration** | Began **1841** (town-level registration dates to **1639**) |

For newly arrived immigrants, the most immediately useful vital records are: births of children born in Massachusetts after arrival, marriages contracted here, and deaths. These are filed at the **town (Boston) level** and at the state level from 1841 onward.

---

### 4. Church Records ⭐ Essential for Irish Catholic immigrants

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — name-indexed |
| **Catholic originals** | Archdiocese of Boston Archives |

The FamilySearch Wiki notes that Catholic parish registers — particularly those of the **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's** — document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward ([Massachusetts Church Records — Boston Area Churches](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)). These registers often predate or supplement sparse civil vital records for newly arrived families and may record the Irish parish of origin. Contact the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** for access.

---

### 5. The Boston *Pilot* — Missing Persons Database

The *Pilot*, an Irish Catholic newspaper, published **arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements** from the 1840s onward for Irish immigrants seeking relatives. The **Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database** (covering 1831–1921) is searchable online and documents tens of thousands of Irish immigrants by name. This is one of the few sources that may name an Irish county of origin. Search it at [infowanted.bc.edu](https://infowanted.bc.edu).

---

### 6. Federal Census Records

| Census | Coverage | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **1840** | Names head of household only; other members appear as age/sex tallies | Immigrants arrived before 1840 or early in the decade may appear |
| **1850** | Names every individual; records age, birthplace (country-level), occupation | Best snapshot of settled immigrant families — includes country of birth |

Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1850 census is the first to name all individuals and give birthplace, making it a crucial anchor for the 1840s immigration cohort.

---

### 7. Probate Records

| | |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch collection** | [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — name-indexed |

Probate files name heirs, relatives, and sometimes birthplace — useful for immigrants who died in Massachusetts after establishing themselves.

---

### 8. Military Records

Immigrants who served in the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) or later conflicts may have federal service records and pension files. **Fold3** (fold3.com) holds military service records; the **Massachusetts State Archives** holds state adjutant general records.

---

### Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Passenger list originals (NARA RG 36); pre-1906 federal court naturalizations |
| **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** | Statewide vital records (post-1841); state court naturalizations |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers — baptisms, marriages, burials |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections: passenger lists, naturalization, vital, church, probate |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists; census records; supplementary sources |
| **Newspapers.com / Boston Pilot database** | Historical newspapers; Irish missing-persons advertisements |
| **Find A Grave (findagrave.com)** | Cemetery records and headstone photographs |
| **NARA / archives.gov** | Passenger list originals; military records |

---

### Key Quirks and Research Strategies

1. **Passenger lists alone rarely give Irish townland or parish.** 1840s lists record country of origin, not the specific locality. To find Irish origins, work from the passenger list to naturalization records, church registers (which sometimes note the Irish parish), and the *Pilot* missing-persons database.

2. **The digitized Port of Boston volume (003345210) is only 3% name-indexed.** Search it via **full-text search** (available) or browse image by image. The parent collection (id: 1784312) has broader name indexing — start there, then go to the volume for gaps.

3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across courts.** Search federal, state, and local court records for Suffolk County; do not assume an immigrant's naturalization is in one place.

4. **Massachusetts vital registration was two-tiered.** Town clerks recorded vital events from 1639; statewide registration was added in 1841. Both series exist for the 1840s — search both town records and the statewide series.

5. **The FamilySearch wiki_place_page tool returned only a generic guide** for Massachusetts — not the Massachusetts-specific research pages. For deeper strategy, visit the Massachusetts research pages on FamilySearch Wiki directly: the [Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration) and [Massachusetts Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records) pages were the most informative sources returned by this survey.

6. **Consider Irish origin records as a parallel track.** Since 1840s passenger lists rarely give townland-level origins, you may need to work backwards from Massachusetts records to identify the Irish county, then pivot to Irish civil registration (began 1864), Catholic parish registers, Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864), and Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) to trace the family in Ireland.

## Locality Research Guide: Native American Tribes in Indian Territory (Oklahoma), ~1830–1900

### Jurisdictional Context

In the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was **Indian Territory** — not yet a U.S. state or territory in the conventional sense. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 compelled the relocation of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) from the southeastern U.S. via the Trail of Tears. These nations governed themselves with their own tribal governments, courts, newspapers, and schools.

A critical split occurred in **1890**: the federal government carved the western half of Indian Territory into **Oklahoma Territory**, leaving the Five Civilized Tribes' lands as the eastern "Indian Territory" proper. This means mid-to-late 1800s records may be filed under either jurisdiction depending on where and when an event occurred. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until **1907**, when both territories merged.

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** Records created before 1907 appear under "Indian Territory" — *not* "Oklahoma" — in most databases. Search both place names on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and NARA's catalog.

---

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls — ⭐ The Essential Starting Point

These are the most genealogically powerful records for this research.

| Roll | Dates | Tribes | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Dawes Rolls** | 1898–1914 | All Five Civilized Tribes | FamilySearch, Ancestry, NARA Fort Worth |
| **Old Settler Cherokee Roll** | 1851 | Western Cherokee | FamilySearch |
| **Drennen Roll** | 1852 | Cherokee (annuity) | FamilySearch |
| **Pre-Dawes tribal censuses** | 1860s–1890s | Varies by tribe | NARA RG 75; FamilySearch |

The **Dawes Rolls** record name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation. They are the gateway record for Five Civilized Tribes research, even though they postdate the mid-1800s — they often include parents' names and references to earlier enrollment attempts. Physical originals are at **NARA Fort Worth**; they are indexed online at both FamilySearch and Ancestry.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959*
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
- 567,890 records | 283,945 images | **Indexed — searchable by name**

**Digitized volume found via volume search:** Image group 002298871 — *Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870*
- 940 images | **99% name-indexed** | Full-text searchable
- Access: FamilySearch (browse + record search)

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** The Dawes Rolls excluded many people — some were denied enrollment due to blood quantum disputes, missed deadlines, or political conflicts within tribal governments. An ancestor's absence from the Dawes Roll does not mean they were not tribal members; look for pre-Dawes rolls and correspondence files (Dawes Commission case files at NARA Fort Worth).

---

### 2. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records — NARA Record Group 75

The BIA maintained continuous records from the 1820s onward, including:

- **Annuity payment rolls** (pre-removal through 1800s) — list individuals by family, often the only mid-1800s "census" for a tribe
- **Agency correspondence** — letters naming individuals, family disputes, deaths, land claims
- **Farmer/employee records** and **school enrollment lists**
- **Census cards** submitted to the Dawes Commission

**Repository:** National Archives, Washington D.C. (Record Group 75) and **NARA Fort Worth** (Indian Territory field records). NARA's online catalog at https://catalog.archives.gov/ lets you search by tribe name and agency.

**Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized portions of BIA records. Cross-check with NARA's physical holdings for undigitized series.

---

### 3. Land Records — Allotments and Early Patents

Following the Dawes Act (1887) and Curtis Act (1898), tribal lands were allotted to individual members. **Allotment jackets** (case files) often contain birth dates, family relationships, and testimony about ancestry.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907*
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- 234,567 records | 117,283 images | **Indexed — searchable by name**

Also consult the **BLM General Land Office** (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) for federal land patents.

---

### 4. Mission and Church Records — 1820s Onward

Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries operated among the Five Civilized Tribes from the 1820s, maintaining registers of converts, baptisms, marriages, burials, and school students. These are often the only pre-1870 vital records available for Native families.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965*
🔗 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321
- 123,456 records | 61,728 images | **Indexed — searchable by name**

Denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society) hold original registers not yet fully digitized.

---

### 5. Federal Censuses — Limited Coverage for Indian Territory

Standard U.S. federal censuses (1840–1880) **did not reliably enumerate Indian Territory**. Special Indian censuses and tribal rolls served as the substitute:

- **1860, 1880, 1900 federal censuses** included some Indian Territory enumeration, but coverage is uneven — verify with the actual census images, not just indexes
- **1900 federal census** is the first to systematically enumerate Indian Territory alongside the Dawes Roll process
- State/territorial censuses: Oklahoma Territory (not Indian Territory) held its own censuses in 1890, 1897, 1900, and 1907 — these cover western Oklahoma only

For **mortality data** (deaths in the year preceding the census), the 1850–1885 mortality schedules are on Ancestry and FamilySearch, but again, Indian Territory coverage is sparse.

---

### 6. Tribal Nation Records (Self-Governed)

Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained its own government records:

- **Cherokee Nation:** Court records, citizenship rolls, newspaper (*Cherokee Phoenix*, later *Cherokee Advocate*), school records — many held at the Oklahoma Historical Society and the Cherokee Nation Archives in Tahlequah
- **Choctaw Nation:** Council records, citizenship rolls — Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Chickasaw Nation:** Council minutes, citizenship applications — Oklahoma Historical Society and Chickasaw Nation archives
- **Creek (Muscogee) Nation:** Town (talwa) records, citizenship rolls — Oklahoma Historical Society
- **Seminole Nation:** Enrollment records — NARA Fort Worth

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** Tribal nations are sovereign — some records are held *by the tribes themselves*, not at NARA or a state archive. Contact tribal historic preservation offices directly. The Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, and Chickasaw Nation all have active genealogy programs and online research portals.

---

### 7. Military Records

Native men from Indian Territory served in the Civil War on both Union and Confederate sides. The **Indian Home Guard** (Union) and **Confederate Indian regiments** generated service records and pension files.

- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/): Indexed Civil War service records, including Indian Territory units
- **NARA:** Pension application files often contain family information (widow's pensions list children, parents)
- FamilySearch collection: *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (id: 2134789) — post-dates the mid-1800s but may document marriages of Civil War veterans

---

### 8. Treaties — The Legal Framework

Treaties between tribes and the U.S. government are primary documents that name signatories and define tribal membership. Key mid-1800s treaties include the **Treaty of New Echota (1835, Cherokee)** and post-Civil War reconstruction treaties (1866). Full treaty texts are at:

- **NARA** (Record Group 11)
- **Oklahoma Historical Society**: https://www.okhistory.org/
- **University of Oklahoma Western History Collections**: https://libraries.ou.edu/content/western-history-collections

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Fort Worth** | Dawes Rolls, BIA field records, allotment files, tribal court records | In-person; portions on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **NARA Washington D.C.** | BIA Record Group 75 (agency correspondence, annuity rolls) | In-person; portions on Fold3 |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Tribal nation records, newspapers, photographs | In-person + online catalog: okhistory.org |
| **FamilySearch** | Indian Censuses & Rolls, land records, church records | Free online |
| **Ancestry** | Dawes Rolls, federal censuses, Fold3 partnership | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | BIA records, Civil War military records | Subscription |
| **Tribal archives** | Nation-specific citizenship, court, school records | Contact tribe directly |

---

### Digitization Coverage Assessment

| Record Type | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Tribal enrollment rolls (1851–1959) | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
| Tribal enrollment cards 1840–1870 | ✅ 99% name-indexed + full-text searchable |
| Early land records (1834–1907) | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
| Mission/church records (1820–1965) | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
