## Pennsylvania Quaker Genealogy — Locality Guide
**Focus:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) · Late 1700s (c. 1770–1800)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded as a Quaker haven by William Penn in 1681 and was a **colony** until statehood in 1787. For the late 1700s you are straddling the colonial and early national periods — county courthouses and the state Land Office in Harrisburg are the civil anchors, but **civil registration did not exist**: Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide vital registration until 1906. For births, marriages, and deaths in this era, **Quaker meeting records are the primary source**, not government registers.

The densest Quaker concentrations were in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties**. By the late 1700s some families were also moving into Lancaster, York, and newly-formed western counties — track county formation dates carefully, as records follow the county that existed at the time of the event.

---

### 1. Quaker Meeting Records ⭐ *Primary source for this research*

Quaker monthly meetings kept some of the most meticulous pre-civil-registration records in America. What they documented:

| Record Type | What's in It |
|---|---|
| **Births & deaths** | Recorded in meeting registers, substituting for baptism/burial records |
| **Marriages** | Performed within the meeting; certificates were **signed by every attendee** — a unique list of witnesses that can reveal extended kin networks |
| **Certificates of removal** | Issued when a member transferred to another monthly meeting; traces migration between meetings and into new counties or states |
| **Disownments** | Records disciplinary proceedings (e.g., marrying outside the faith, joining the military during the Revolution); name the individual and often family members |
| **Monthly/quarterly/yearly meeting minutes** | Administrative records that name individuals in a variety of contexts |

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Church Records: Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))*

#### What FamilySearch has digitized

**Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800**
- Image Group: `001188322` · 145 images
- **Digitization level: Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable
- You must browse page by page; there is no name search
- This is the **only** Quaker-specific digitized volume that the FamilySearch volume search returned for Pennsylvania in the late 1700s — a significant coverage gap

FamilySearch has also **microfilmed** many individual monthly meeting registers and minute books (per the FamilySearch Wiki), but the volume search did not surface them as digitized and name-indexed for this period. They may exist as browse-only microfilm scans or physical microfilm only.

#### Major repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) | Largest collection of American Quaker records; original meeting registers, minutes, certificates | On-site research; some materials available on microfilm via interlibrary loan |
| **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA) | Significant PA Quaker manuscript collections | On-site research |
| **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives** | Records of the central organizing body covering most PA meetings | Contact for access |

#### Published abstracts — critical shortcut

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes** abstracts thousands of Quaker meeting records from Pennsylvania and neighboring states. This is often the fastest entry point before going to original microfilm or manuscript. Check if your library holds it or if a digitized version is accessible through your genealogical society. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Church Records: Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts))*

---

### 2. Civil Marriage Records

Even though Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration, **marriage licenses and bonds were recorded at the county courthouse** from the colonial period onward.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))*

**Note:** Quakers did **not** obtain civil marriage licenses — their marriages were solemnized within the meeting. Do not expect a courthouse marriage record for a Quaker couple; the meeting marriage certificate is the authoritative record.

FamilySearch collections that overlap the late 1700s (for non-Quaker neighbors or mixed-faith situations):

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 |

---

### 3. Probate Records

Wills, estate inventories, administration bonds, and guardianship records are held at the **county Register of Wills** from the colonial period onward. These records begin early and are an excellent supplement to Quaker records — a Quaker decedent's will may name children, grandchildren, and neighbors.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))*

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 |

---

### 4. Land Records

Pennsylvania land records begin with William Penn's original grants (1681). The **Pennsylvania State Archives / Land Office in Harrisburg** holds warrant, survey, and patent records. County deed books begin at each county's formation date.

For Quaker families, land records are especially valuable because:
- Quakers frequently settled in clusters and conveyed land to fellow members
- Land transactions can corroborate removal certificates when a family relocated

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))*

---

### 5. Tax Records (Pre-1790 Census Substitute)

Pennsylvania tax assessment lists and tax duplicates survive from the **1690s** in some counties and are the primary substitute for census records before the first federal enumeration in 1790. The 1693 Chester County tax list is one of the earliest surviving colonial examples. Tax records can confirm residence and approximate household wealth.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))*

---

### 6. Federal Census (1790 onward)

The **1790 federal census** is the first for Pennsylvania and lists heads of household with a count of household members by age/sex category — not individual names. Earlier censuses do not exist; tax lists and Quaker meeting records fill the gap before 1790.

---

### 7. Military Records

Quakers were **pacifists** and typically refused military service. During the American Revolution (1775–1783), many Pennsylvania Quakers were **disowned** by their meetings for bearing arms or paying commutation fees. If an ancestor disappears from meeting records in the 1770s–1780s, check for a disownment — and then Revolutionary War pension files at NARA (accessible via [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)) for evidence they served despite their faith.

---

### Research Strategy Summary

1. **Start with Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** — abstracts are faster than raw microfilm.
2. **Identify the specific monthly meeting**: Quaker records are organized by monthly meeting, not county. Determine which meeting your family belonged to before searching. Meetings in the late 1700s include Philadelphia Monthly Meeting, Abington, Gwynedd, Horsham, Concord, Nottingham, and many others.
3. **Browse the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes on FamilySearch** (image group `001188322`) — 145 browse-only images covering 1750–1800.
4. **Contact Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore)** for the specific monthly meeting's original registers and minutes — this is where the bulk of the records live.
5. **Pull the certificate of removal** if the family migrated — it names the destination meeting and can trace the family into New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, or westward into Ohio.
6. **Supplement with probate and tax records** at the county level to build a corroborating documentary trail.
7. **Check the 1790 federal census** for household composition, then use pre-1790 tax lists for earlier evidence of residence.

---

### Key Quirks and Cautions

- **No civil vital registration** in Pennsylvania until 1906 — Quaker meeting records are the primary birth/marriage/death source for this community and era.
- **Quaker marriages were not recorded in civil registers.** County marriage licenses do not cover Friends couples.
- **County formation matters.** Chester County (1682) was the mother county for much of southeastern Pennsylvania — records for events before daughter counties were formed (e.g., Delaware County formed from Chester in 1789, Montgomery County formed from Philadelphia in 1784) may be filed under the parent county.
- **Disownments during the Revolution (1775–1783) are common** and may explain gaps in meeting membership records for an ancestor.
- **Certificates of removal are migration evidence.** A family moving from Philadelphia Monthly Meeting to a western Pennsylvania or Ohio meeting would receive one — it is direct documentary proof of the move.
- **Browse-only gap on FamilySearch.** Only one Quaker-specific digitized volume was found for Pennsylvania in this period, and it is 0% indexed. Most records require either contacting Swarthmore/Haverford directly or ordering microfilm.

## Locality Research Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry (c. 1870–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh is the county seat. During the late 1800s Pittsburgh became the center of American steel production, drawing massive immigrant labor — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers poured into the city and surrounding mill towns. Allegheny County is the sole relevant jurisdiction for this period; no boundary splits affect the research trail.

> **Quirk — vital registration timing:** Allegheny County began recording births and deaths from **1870**, well ahead of Pennsylvania's statewide mandate in **1906**. Do not assume no pre-1906 records exist — search the county series first.
> ([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County Genealogy — Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))

> **Quirk — 1890 census destroyed:** The 1890 federal census is largely destroyed nationwide. Bridge the 1880–1900 gap with Pittsburgh city directories and church registers.

---

### 1. Industrial & Occupational Records ⭐ *(primary focus)*

These are the most distinctive sources for steel-era research and are partially physical-only.

| Source | Location | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** (Carnegie Steel and others — fragmentary) | Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives | Physical; not comprehensively indexed |
| **Union membership lists** | Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel archives | Physical; fragmentary |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Physical; some digitized |
| **Pittsburgh city directories** (occupation listed; begin 1813) | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; Ancestry.com | Physical + some online |

> The FamilySearch Wiki's Allegheny County page notes these records directly: ([Allegheny County — Industrial and Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))

**Company records are fragmentary** — survival depends entirely on the firm. The Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives are the first stops; expect gaps. City directories are often the most reliable occupational record because they were published annually and list name, occupation, and address.

**Federal census occupation columns** (1870, 1880, 1900) list each person's stated occupation and are fully searchable — see Census section below.

---

### 2. Vital Records

**Births & Deaths**
- Allegheny County recorded births and deaths from **1870** (county level), before statewide registration in 1906.
- Records held at the Allegheny County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- FamilySearch's **Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968** (collection [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), 4,218,763 records, fully indexed with images) covers deaths from 1906 onward — useful for deaths that occurred just after the target window.

**Marriages**
- Marriage licenses from **1885** are at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- Three indexed FamilySearch collections overlap the target period:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records | Date Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 524,189 | 1885–1950 |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 312,045 | 1677–1950 |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 198,765 | 1700–1900 |

> Pre-1885 marriages are best traced through church records (see below).

---

### 3. Census Records

| Census Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1870 | Lists occupation, birthplace, real/personal estate value |
| 1880 | Lists occupation, birthplace of parents, relationship to head |
| 1890 | **Largely destroyed** — use city directories and church records to fill the gap |
| 1900 | Lists occupation, immigration year, years in the U.S., naturalization status |

Allegheny County federal census records survive from 1800. The **1880 and 1900 censuses are especially valuable** for industrial workers: they record birthplace of parents and (in 1900) immigration year and naturalization status — critical for tracing immigrant steel workers.
([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County — Census and Naturalization](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))

All censuses 1870–1900 are available name-indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

### 4. Church Records

Catholic parishes serving specific ethnic communities are often the richest source for immigrant steel-worker families, because civil vital registration was incomplete in the early part of this period.

- **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** holds baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the 1840s onward for parishes that served Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and Irish communities.
- Registers are typically in Latin or the community's language.
- Protestant denominations (Presbyterian, Methodist, German Lutheran, German Reformed) also served earlier-arriving workers; their registers are more scattered — check the FamilySearch Catalog by county for microfilmed holdings.

> Approach by **ethnic community first**: identify the worker's nationality from the census, then find the parish that served that community in the specific Pittsburgh neighborhood or mill town.
([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County — Vital and Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))

---

### 5. Naturalization & Immigration

- **Naturalization records** from the Allegheny County **Court of Common Pleas (1798–1930)** are held at the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region).
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across multiple courts (federal and county); the county court series is the primary source for Pittsburgh workers.
- **Passenger lists** (arriving immigrants) are at NARA and searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Cross the immigration year from the 1900 census against passenger arrival lists.

([FamilySearch Wiki: Allegheny County — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))

---

### 6. Probate Records

- FamilySearch **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196), 893,214 records) covers Allegheny County wills, inventories, and administrations and is name-indexed with images.
- Probate records can confirm family relationships and provide an economic snapshot of a steel worker's estate.

---

### 7. Newspapers & City Directories

- **Newspapers.com** and the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** hold Pittsburgh-area newspapers. Obituaries and labor strike coverage are particularly useful for industrial workers.
- **Pittsburgh city directories** (Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh; also partly on Ancestry) begin in 1813 and list name, occupation, and address annually — the best substitute for the destroyed 1890 census and a strong occupational supplement to any census year.

---

### 8. Military Records

- Veterans of the Civil War (1861–65) who were working the mills in the 1870s–1900s may have **pension files** at NARA (searchable on Fold3 and Ancestry) — these contain rich family data including wife's name, children, and addresses.
- **Spanish-American War (1898)** service records are at NARA.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Industrial/company records, immigration records, newspapers | In-person; some online finding aids |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** (Homestead, PA) | Steel company and union records | In-person; contact for access |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1813+), local history, newspapers | In-person; some digital |
| **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Ethnic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | In-person; appointment recommended |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Marriage licenses (1885+), naturalization records | In-person |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA)** | Naturalization records (Court of Common Pleas, 1798–1930), passenger lists, military | In-person + online (Ancestry, Fold3) |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Factory inspector reports, county vital records, state census | In-person; some online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Marriages, probate, death certs (1906+), census, catalog of microfilm | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |

---

### Digitization Assessment

| Record Type | Status |
|---|---|
| Federal census 1870–1900 | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch, Ancestry) |
| County marriages 1885–1900 | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1921317) |
| Compiled marriages to 1900 | ✅ Indexed, no images (FamilySearch collection 1502909) |
| Probate records | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1999196) |
| Death certificates | ✅ Indexed + images — but **starts 1906**, outside target window |
| Naturalization records | ⚠️ Partially indexed on Ancestry; physical originals at NARA Philadelphia |
| Church registers | ⚠️ Fragmentary — some on FamilySearch microfilm; many physical-only at diocese |
| Company/union records | 🔴 Largely physical-only at Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel; fragmentary survival |
| City directories | ⚠️ Some years on Ancestry; Carnegie Library holds the full run |
| Factory inspector reports | 🔴 Physical at Pennsylvania State Archives |

---

### Research Strategy for Steel-Industry Families

1. **Start with the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses** — they give occupation, birthplace of parents, and (in 1900) immigration year, which anchors the research trail.
2. **Use city directories annually** to track residential moves between census years and confirm occupations — especially critical for the 1890 gap.
3. **Contact the Heinz History Center** for company employment and union records; be prepared for gaps, but a surviving employment card or union ledger entry can be transformative.
4. **Identify the ethnic parish** from the census birthplace and neighborhood, then request the register from the Catholic Diocese Archives or check FamilySearch microfilm holdings.
5. **Pull naturalization records** from NARA Philadelphia — they often name the immigrant's home village, which opens up European research.
6. **Check pension files** (Fold3/Ancestry) if the ancestor was old enough to have served in the Civil War before arriving at the mills.

# Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic
## Locality Research Guide

**Jurisdiction:** Philadelphia County / City of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
**Standard place:** Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States (County); formed 1682
**Target period:** 1793, with bracketing searches in 1780–1810
**Population context:** Approximately 50,000 residents at the time of the epidemic (Wikipedia); roughly 5,000 — one-tenth of the city — died between August and November 1793.

---

### Jurisdictional Notes

Philadelphia was simultaneously a city and a county from its founding in 1682, making it unusual: city and county records are often identical. Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration of vital events until 1906** — confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki (source: [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)). For 1793, **church registers are the primary source of birth, marriage, and death documentation**. There is no civil death certificate to find for an epidemic victim.

---

## Epidemic-Specific Records ⚠️ Start Here

These sources exist specifically because of the 1793 outbreak and are the highest-yield starting point for families affected by it.

### 1. Mathew Carey's Published Account of the Dead
Carey's *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793 and multiple subsequent editions) contains a **named list of victims**. This is a published, widely held document — available at HSP, the Library Company of Philadelphia, and reprinted by multiple libraries. It is among the most direct ways to confirm a death during the epidemic.
- **Access:** Physical copies at HSP and Library Company of Philadelphia; also digitized via Google Books and HathiTrust.
- **Digitization level:** Full text available online — searchable by name.

### 2. Committee of the Citizens — Minutes and Reports
Mayor Matthew Clarkson appointed a citizens' committee to manage the crisis. Their minutes and reports document relief distributions, deaths, orphaned children, and the names of those who assisted or fled. These manuscript records are held by the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**.
- **Access:** Physical only; no online equivalent confirmed by tool survey. Request through the archives.
- **Digitization level:** Physical/manuscript only.

### 3. Bush Hill Hospital Records
Bush Hill was the city's fever hospital. Patient records are fragmentary but some survive. Held by HSP.
- **Access:** Physical/manuscript. Coverage is incomplete — rapid epidemic conditions limited record-keeping.

---

## Church Records — Primary Vital Source

The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that Philadelphia's church records are the **primary source of vital information** before 1906 and that many early national registers have been transcribed and published. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church registers (source: [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)).

The following congregations were active in Philadelphia in 1793. Their burial registers are the chief death-documentation sources:

| Congregation | Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Christ Church | Anglican/Episcopal | One of Philadelphia's largest; burial register is well-preserved |
| Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') | Lutheran (Swedish) | One of the oldest churches in the city; active burial register |
| St. Peter's | Episcopal | Daughter church of Christ Church |
| Friends (Quakers) | Society of Friends | Multiple meetings; Quaker records are highly systematic |
| First Presbyterian | Presbyterian | Active congregation |
| St. Mary's / St. Joseph's | Roman Catholic | Separate registers for each parish |
| German Lutheran / German Reformed | Lutheran / Reformed | German-speaking congregation; registers may be in German |
| Mikveh Israel | Jewish | Active Jewish congregation; separate record-keeping tradition |
| African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas | Episcopal | Founded 1792; African-American congregation |
| Mother Bethel (African Methodist Episcopal) | Methodist | Founded 1793; African-American congregation |

> **Critical quirk:** During the epidemic, burials were so rapid that many victims were interred without clergy attendance or church registration. Absence from a church register does not confirm survival — cross-check the Carey list and Committee minutes.

> **Quirk — German-language records:** German Lutheran and German Reformed registers from this period are typically written in German. A researcher must be able to read 18th-century German script or engage a translator.

**Access:** Many registers have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. Some have been transcribed and published by the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania. Originals are held at the respective church archives or, in many cases, deposited with HSP or the Presbyterian Historical Society. Browse the FamilySearch catalog under "Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania — Church Records" for specific microfilm holdings.

---

## Federal Census Records

- **1790 census** (taken before the epidemic): Establishes the household composition *before* the outbreak. Name-indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1800 census** (taken after the epidemic): Comparing 1790 and 1800 household compositions can reveal disappearances consistent with epidemic death. Also name-indexed.

> **Researcher note:** Thousands of residents *fled* Philadelphia during the epidemic (August–November 1793) and returned afterward. A person present in 1790 but absent in 1800 may have died, emigrated, or simply relocated within or near the city. The census alone cannot confirm epidemic death.

- **Digitization level:** Both censuses are **fully indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

## Probate Records (High Priority for 1793 Deaths)

Every death that left an estate generates probate activity. The 1793 epidemic created a surge in will probations, estate administrations, and orphans' court filings. These records will name decedents, heirs, creditors, and guardians of minor children.

**FamilySearch collection (confirmed by tool survey):**
- **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** — Collection ID 1999196 — [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)
  - 893,214 indexed records; 446,607 images
  - **Digitization level: Indexed + images** — name-searchable online

> Philadelphia's Orphans' Court, which handled guardianships of children whose parents died, is especially relevant for epidemic families. Orphans' court minutes from 1793–1795 would show children left without parents.

---

## Marriage Records

Two FamilySearch collections confirmed by the tool survey cover the 1793 period:

- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** — Collection ID 1571957 — [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)
  - 312,045 indexed records; 156,023 images
  - **Digitization level: Indexed + images**
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** — Collection ID 1502909 — [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)
  - 198,765 indexed records; **0 images** — index only, no images confirmed
  - **Digitization level: Index only (no images in this collection)**

---

## Tax Records

Pennsylvania county tax records (ground tax, property tax) exist for Philadelphia from the colonial period. Tax lists from the late 1780s and 1790s document heads of household by name and property value, and can establish residence before and after the epidemic.

- **Access:** Philadelphia tax records are held at the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP. Some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch — search the FamilySearch catalog under "Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania — Taxation."
- **Digitization level:** Variable; many are browse-only or microfilm-only. No specific Philadelphia tax collection was returned by the FamilySearch collection survey for the 1793 window.

---

## Newspapers

Philadelphia had several newspapers in 1793 that published death notices and epidemic updates, including the *Pennsylvania Gazette*, *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, and *Gazette of the United States*. Death notices in these papers are a direct source for named victims.

- **Access:** Historical newspaper access via **Newspapers.com** and the **Library of Congress Chronicling America** digitization project. The Library Company of Philadelphia and HSP hold original runs.
- **Digitization level:** Chronicling America coverage of Philadelphia papers from this period is partial — keyword-searchable where digitized. Newspapers.com holds additional content.

---

## Land and Property Records

Philadelphia deed books are held at the Philadelphia City Archives (as the recorder of deeds). Rapid estate settlements following deaths may produce deed transfers in 1793–1795.

- **Access:** Physical records at Philadelphia City Archives. Some early deed records are indexed in published abstracts. FamilySearch microfilm holdings exist; search the catalog under "Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania — Land Records."
- **Digitization level:** Likely browse-only or microfilm-only for this period based on the tool survey.

---

## Military Records

The 1793 period falls in the post-Revolutionary, pre-War of 1812 window. If an ancestor served in the Revolutionary War, **pension files** at NARA (Record Group 15) can document survivors and family composition through the 1790s. Widows' pension claims filed after a veteran's death provide family detail.

- **Access:** Pension files at NARA; indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on Fold3.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City government records; Committee of Citizens minutes; deed records; city death registers (post-1860) | In-person; some records online |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscript collections; Committee minutes; Bush Hill records; many church register transcriptions; Carey account | In-person; HSP Digital Library for selected items |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** | Published indexes to Philadelphia church records; compiled genealogies | In-person; publications widely held |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Colonial and early national printed sources; Carey pamphlet; newspapers | In-person; some digitized |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society** | Presbyterian church registers | In-person |
| **Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore College)** | Quaker meeting records | In-person; some microfilmed |
| **FamilySearch** | Probate Records 1683–1994; Civil Marriages 1677–1950; Compiled Marriages 1700–1900; extensive microfilm catalog | Online (FamilySearch.org) |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Revolutionary War pension files; federal census | Online (Fold3, Ancestry) and in-person |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1790 and 1800 federal census; newspaper collections | Subscription online |

---

## Research Quirks and Warnings

1. **No civil death records exist for 1793.** Pennsylvania's statewide registration began in 1906. Church burial registers, the Carey list, and Committee minutes are the only near-contemporary death documentation.

2. **Flight vs. death.** Thousands of Philadelphians fled the city during August–November 1793. An ancestor absent from post-epidemic records may have died, may have settled elsewhere after evacuation, or may have returned under a slightly different name rendering.

3. **Rapid burials reduced church registration.** Some victims were buried without clergy attendance, especially in the worst weeks of the epidemic. Potter's field and informal burials supplement church registers.

4. **Potter's field burials.** Philadelphia's potter's field (the municipal burial ground for the poor and unregistered dead) received epidemic victims. These records, if they survive, are held at the Philadelphia City Archives, but coverage is fragmentary.

5. **African-American families.** Black Philadelphians, including members of Richard Allen's African Methodist Episcopal congregation and Absalom Jones's African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas (both founded 1792–1793), played a major role in epidemic nursing and suffered significant losses. Records for these congregations are held at their respective church archives and at HSP.

6. **German-language registers.** German Lutheran and German Reformed registers from 1793 are typically in German. Plan for translation.

7. **The 1800 census is the first post-epidemic count** — compare it to 1790 to identify missing household members, but confirm deaths in church records before concluding epidemic mortality.

8. **FamilySearch collection survey note:** The `collections_search` tool returned 6 Pennsylvania collections for the 1750–1830 window; the first entry (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is flagged as a synthetic test fixture and should not be treated as a real collection. The five remaining real collections are documented above.

---

## Suggested Research Sequence for 1793 Epidemic Families

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's list** — confirm death during the epidemic.
2. **Search the relevant church burial register** — identify the burial date and any surviving family noted.
3. **Pull probate records (FamilySearch collection 1999196)** — search for an estate administration filed 1793–1796.
4. **Check 1790 and 1800 federal census** — establish pre- and post-epidemic household.
5. **Search Philadelphia newspapers (1793) for death notices.**
6. **Contact HSP and Philadelphia City Archives** for Committee of Citizens minutes and any manuscript sources.
7. **Check Orphans' Court minutes (HSP / Philadelphia City Archives)** for any guardianship established for minor children.
8. **Search tax records** before and after 1793 to track property and residency changes.

# Locality Research Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire Era (c. 1850–1890)

## Jurisdiction Summary

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Place** | Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States |
| **County formed** | 1831 (from Putnam County) |
| **City incorporated** | 1837 |
| **Target period** | ~1850–1890, centered on the October 8–10, 1871 fire |
| **Key disaster** | Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871 |

**The central genealogical challenge:** The fire killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and incinerated the Cook County Courthouse — destroying deeds, birth and death registers, court records, probate files, tax rolls, and many church registers. Almost all pre-October 10, 1871 official county records are gone. Everything before that date requires substitute sources.

---

## ⚠️ Critical Quirk: The Pre-Fire / Post-Fire Divide

The fire on October 8–10, 1871 is the single most important fact shaping your research strategy:

- **Before October 10, 1871:** County-level official records are largely destroyed. Do not expect to find original deeds, court files, or county vital records. Use the substitute sources listed below.
- **After October 10, 1871:** County record-keeping resumed, and civil registration of births, deaths, and marriages began. These post-fire records survive in good numbers and many are digitized on FamilySearch.
- **The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived** because the original schedules were held in Washington, D.C., not at the county courthouse — this is your most important pre-fire population snapshot.

---

## Record Classes and Availability

### 1. Federal Census Records
**Availability:** ✅ Indexed + images (pre-fire censuses survived)

The 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses for Chicago are intact — the originals were retained in Washington and were not destroyed. The 1880 census captures the post-fire rebuilt population. Mortality schedules (which list deaths in the year preceding each census) also survived for 1850–1880 and can name fire-era casualties.

- **Access:** FamilySearch (free); Ancestry.com
- **Key tip:** The 1870 census, taken months before the October fire, is your last pre-fire household snapshot. Search it first to establish who was in Chicago and where they lived.

---

### 2. Vital Records (Birth, Death, Marriage)
**Availability:** ✅ Indexed + images (post-fire only; pre-fire records destroyed)

FamilySearch holds three large indexed Cook County collections covering the post-fire era:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Record Count | Date Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 2024189 | ~1,450,000 | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County Death Records | 1913456 | ~980,000 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 1756321 | ~620,000 | 1871–1920 |

- **Access:** FamilySearch (searchable by name)
- **Cook County Clerk's office** also holds original vital records from 1871 onward
- **Pre-fire vital events:** No county civil registration existed before 1871. Use church registers (see below) for baptisms, marriages, and burials before the fire.

---

### 3. Church Records
**Availability:** ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch); physical originals at denominational archives

FamilySearch holds:
- **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925** (Collection ID: 1803978; ~285,000 records)

This collection spans both the pre- and post-fire periods and is the most important source for families' vital events before October 1871. Parishes that survived the fire (or reconstructed their registers) are represented here.

- **Catholic records:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's **Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers. Many Chicago parishes were established by immigrant communities (German, Irish, Polish, Bohemian) and kept registers in their native language.
- **Other denominations:** Check the **Newberry Library** and the relevant denominational archives.
- **Gap warning:** Many church registers were destroyed along with the courthouse. Where a parish register is missing for pre-1871 years, no substitute exists within that church's own records.

---

### 4. Property and Land Records (Burnt Record Act Reconstitutions)
**Availability:** 🔶 Partially indexed (41% name-indexed) + browse-only reconstructed pre-fire copies

This is a uniquely important record class for fire-affected families:

| Volume | Image Group | Coverage | Indexed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Post-fire Property Re-recordings (Burnt Record Act) | 009982111 | 1871–1880, 112 images | 41% name-indexed |
| Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies) | 009982110 | 1865–1871, 38 images | 0% — browse-only |

**The Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register their deeds with the county after the fire. These re-recorded deeds are your primary substitute for pre-fire property ownership. Volume 009982111 (41% indexed) can be searched by name for about half the records; the rest must be browsed image by image.

**Volume 009982110** (reconstructed pre-fire court records) must be browsed image by image — it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable.

- **Chicago Title and Trust Company records** at the **Chicago History Museum** are the other key source for pre-fire property. Insurance company abstracts often preserve chain-of-title information that predates the fire.
- **Access:** FamilySearch (volumes above); Chicago History Museum (in person or contact for access)

---

### 5. Court and Probate Records
**Availability:** 🔴 Largely destroyed pre-fire; microfilm/physical post-fire

The Cook County Courthouse destruction wiped out most pre-1871 probate files, court cases, and naturalizations. For post-fire records:

- **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD)** at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County court records from the post-fire period.
- **Naturalization records** (pre-1906) may appear in federal, state, or local courts. Check both the county court (IRAD) and the U.S. District Court records at **NARA Great Lakes Region** (Chicago).

---

### 6. City Directories
**Availability:** ✅ Physical/microfilm at the Newberry Library; some digitized

City directories for Chicago survive from the 1840s onward — they were not kept at the courthouse and many survived the fire. They list heads of household, occupations, and addresses, making them invaluable for placing families in specific neighborhoods before and after the fire.

- **Access:** **Newberry Library**, Chicago (extensive holdings); some volumes on Ancestry.com and HathiTrust

---

### 7. Newspapers
**Availability:** ✅ Online (subscription)

Chicago newspapers covered the fire extensively, including lists of the dead, missing, and displaced. Post-fire issues also carried property notices related to the Burnt Record Act filings.

- **Newspapers.com** — historical Chicago newspapers
- **Chicago Tribune** archives (available via ProQuest at many libraries)
- **Chicago History Museum** holds additional newspaper holdings

---

### 8. Military Records
**Availability:** ✅ Indexed + images (federal records at NARA and Fold3)

Federal military records were not held at the county courthouse and survived the fire intact.

- **Civil War service records and pension files:** NARA (free images on Fold3 for service records; pensions require a NARA order or Fold3 subscription)
- **Draft registrations:** NARA Great Lakes Region
- **Illinois Adjutant General records** (state service records) may be at the Illinois State Archives, Springfield

---

### 9. Cemetery Records
**Availability:** ✅ Online (FindAGrave, Billion Graves); physical at cemetery offices

Cemetery records were maintained independently of the courthouse and survived. Chicago's major cemeteries — including Graceland, Rosehill, and Calvary (Catholic) — have their own records offices.

- **FindAGrave** (free) covers many Chicago-area burials with photographs
- Direct contact with cemetery offices for pre-digitized records

---

### 10. Insurance and Business Records
**Availability:** Physical — Chicago History Museum

The **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection** at the Chicago History Museum is one of the most important substitute sources for pre-fire property ownership. Insurance company abstracts compiled chain-of-title records before the fire and often predate courthouse deed books.

- **Access:** Chicago History Museum, 1601 N. Clark St., Chicago, IL 60614; contact the research center for appointments

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Indexed church, vital, property, and court record collections (IDs above) | Free online |
| **Newberry Library** (newberry.org) | City directories, maps, manuscripts, local histories | In person / some digital |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance records, Chicago Title & Trust abstracts, photographs, personal papers | In person / research center |
| **IRAD at NEIU** | Cook County court records (post-1871) | In person / contact IRAD |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers | Contact for access |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records (births, deaths, marriages) from 1871 | In person / mail request |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region** (Chicago) | Federal census, naturalization, federal court, military | In person / online via Ancestry/Fold3 |
| **Illinois State Archives** (Springfield) | State-level records, military, land | In person / some online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, various | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Chicago newspapers | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave.com** | Cemetery and burial records | Free |

---

## Recommended Research Order for Fire-Affected Families

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — the last pre-fire household snapshot, originals intact in Washington.
2. **Search FamilySearch's Cook County church records (Collection 1803978)** — the best pre-fire vital record substitute.
3. **Search post-fire vital records (Collections 2024189 / 1913456 / 1756321)** — births, deaths, and marriages from 1871 onward are well-indexed.
4. **Browse FamilySearch Volume 009982111** (Burnt Record Act property re-recordings, 1871–1880) — establishes where a family owned property before the fire.
5. **Check the Chicago History Museum** for insurance/title records and fire-era photographs and newspapers.
6. **Search city directories at the Newberry Library** — year-by-year address and occupation data before and after 1871.
7. **Contact the Bernardin Archives** if your ancestors were Catholic.
8. **Search NARA/Fold3 for military records** — completely unaffected by the fire.

---

## Coverage Gaps to Note

- The **FamilySearch wiki_place_page** for Illinois returned only a generic fallback — Illinois-specific research-tips pages were not accessible via this tool. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) for additional guidance.
- **Population data** for Chicago in this period was not returned by the tool — the 1870 census recorded approximately 299,000 residents, growing to 503,000 by 1880 after massive post-fire rebuilding.
- FamilySearch's **external links** for this place and period are general (Ancestry census, FindAGrave, Fold3, NARA) — no fire-specific curated links were returned, confirming that the specialist fire-era sources (Chicago History Museum, Newberry Library, IRAD) must be accessed directly.
- Pre-fire **probate and court records are almost entirely unrecoverable** — no FamilySearch volumes or indexed collections exist for this material, consistent with its known destruction.

---

*Sources: Wikipedia — Great Chicago Fire; FamilySearch Wiki — Cook County, Illinois Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire and #Repositories); FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search results; external_links_search results.*

## Locality Research Guide: French Colonial Louisiana, 1700s

### Jurisdictional Context

**French Louisiana (La Louisiane)** was an administrative district of New France, with France controlling the territory from roughly 1699 to 1762. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville and became the colonial capital. The colony operated under the **Code Noir**, which regulated slavery and — critically for genealogy — **required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons**, meaning enslaved ancestors may appear in church registers.

**Critical split in 1762:** By the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), France ceded Louisiana *west* of the Mississippi to Spain, and the *eastern* portion to Britain. Spain did not actually take administrative control until **1769**. This means:

- **1699–1762/1769**: Records are in French, under French colonial administration.
- **After 1769**: Records shift to Spanish administration and the Spanish language (west of the Mississippi). Families in the second half of the 1700s will appear in **Spanish colonial records**, not French ones — treat the two halves of the century as separate documentary regimes.

Colonial records were maintained by two institutions: the **Catholic Church** (parish registers) and the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)** (civil and legal records). There was no civil vital registration — the church is the primary source for births, marriages, and deaths.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. Catholic Parish Registers ⭐ *Primary Source*
**What they contain:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons), marriages, and burials. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana, so virtually all family events for the colonial period are recorded here.

**Coverage:** St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from **1720**. Other parishes were established as the colony expanded.

**FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — approximately 987,654 indexed records with ~493,827 images. The colonial-era portion (1718–1769) is a small subset of this large collection. **Access: indexed + images** — searchable by name on FamilySearch.

**Physical originals:** Held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans) and at individual parishes.

> ⚠️ Records are in **French** for the French colonial period, switching to **Spanish** after 1769. You must be able to read 18th-century French ecclesiastical Latin/French script, or work with a translator.

---

#### 2. Superior Council Records (Conseil Supérieur)
**What they contain:** Land grants (concessions), court proceedings, civil contracts, notarial acts, and estate inventories — the civil and legal backbone of French colonial life. These are the primary substitute for civil registration for property, succession, and legal events.

**Repository:** **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint, 400 Esplanade Avenue, New Orleans. Records have been **partially digitized**. Physical access is available to researchers.

**Online access:** Partial — check the Louisiana Historical Center's online catalog before traveling. No dedicated FamilySearch collection for Superior Council records was returned by this survey; treat undigitized portions as **physical-only**.

---

#### 3. New Orleans Notarial Archives
**What they contain:** Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the **1730s onward** — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Marriage contracts in particular can name parents and witnesses, substituting for missing church or civil records.

**Repository:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — provides public access. Some records have been indexed; inquire directly for finding aids.

**Online access:** Limited. This is primarily a **physical repository**. No FamilySearch collection for this archive was found in this survey.

---

#### 4. Probate Records
**What they contain:** Estate inventories, wills, and administration filings. These often name heirs, spouses, and children — invaluable for reconstructing family structure.

**FamilySearch collection:** **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — approximately 456,789 records with ~228,394 images. Coverage begins **1756**, so this collection catches only the final decade of the French colonial period. **Access: indexed + images.**

---

#### 5. Land Grants and Land Records
**What they contain:** French concessions (land grants) document settlement patterns and can identify family heads and neighbors. These follow French legal tradition (not English common law).

**Repositories and access:**
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** series — published, widely available in libraries and online; covers confirmed colonial-era land grants.
- **Louisiana State Land Office** — holds original French and Spanish land grant documentation.
- **FamilySearch Wiki:** [Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) covers this topic.

---

#### 6. French Colonial Census Rolls and Administrative Correspondence
**What they contain:** Colonial census rolls (recoupements) periodically enumerated heads of household, sometimes listing family members, occupations, and enslaved persons. Administrative correspondence names colonists in various contexts.

**Repository:** **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — the primary repository for French colonial administrative records for Louisiana. These records are **not on FamilySearch**; access is in person in France or through ANOM's online catalog (some records have been digitized and posted at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)).

> ⚠️ For serious French colonial research, ANOM is essential and cannot be bypassed.

---

#### 7. Military Records
French colonial Louisiana had military detachments, and soldiers appear in muster rolls and administrative records — primarily at **ANOM**. The **National Archives (NARA)** holds some later territorial-era military records, but its coverage of the French colonial period is minimal.

---

#### 8. Cemetery and Burial Records
**Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has cemetery transcriptions for Louisiana, including some historic New Orleans cemeteries. For the colonial period, burial entries in **Catholic parish registers** are more reliable than surviving cemetery inscriptions.

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (collection 1612905) | Church records 1718–1925 | Free online, indexed |
| FamilySearch (collection 2078341) | Probate records 1756–1984 | Free online, indexed |
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans | Superior Council records, church records | Physical + partial online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives | Notarial acts from 1730s | Physical, some indexed |
| ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France | Census rolls, admin correspondence | Physical + partial online |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Land grants (French & Spanish) | Physical/state agency |
| American State Papers: Public Lands | Confirmed colonial land grants | Widely available online/libraries |

---

### Key Research Quirks

1. **The 1762/1769 split is a documentary divide.** Families present before 1762 may appear in both French and (after 1769) Spanish records. Do not assume one regime's records are sufficient — check both.

2. **No civil vital registration existed.** For births, marriages, and deaths, the Catholic parish register is your only source. If the parish register is missing or destroyed, there is no parallel civil record to fall back on.

3. **Enslaved persons in church registers.** The Code Noir required baptism of enslaved people, so registers may be your only documentary trace of enslaved ancestors. Entries typically record the enslaver's name, not a surname for the enslaved person.

4. **Records are in 18th-century French.** Ecclesiastical Latin also appears in sacramental formulas. Plan for translation assistance.

5. **ANOM is non-negotiable for colonial administration.** French colonial census rolls and official correspondence are in France, not Louisiana. A research plan that skips ANOM will miss a major class of evidence.

6. **The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Louisiana-specific research guide** in this survey (all four wiki place-page sections returned generic content). Check [FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) directly for updates to online availability.

---

### Starting Points

1. **Identify the parish** where your ancestor lived — colonial Louisiana was organized by Catholic parishes, not counties. Records are held at the parish level.
2. **Search FamilySearch collection 1612905** (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925) for baptism, marriage, and burial entries.
3. **Search FamilySearch collection 2078341** (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) if the ancestor died after 1756.
4. **Contact the Louisiana Historical Center** for Superior Council and notarial records if FamilySearch results are thin.
5. **Search ANOM online** ([anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)) for the ancestor's name in colonial census rolls and correspondence.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Mining Region (Late 1800s — ca. 1850–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Core counties:** Schuylkill (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton), Luzerne (formed 1786), Lackawanna (formed 1878 from Luzerne), Carbon (formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton), and Northumberland (formed 1772)
- **Administrative centers:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe/Mauch Chunk (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population:** Schuylkill County grew from roughly 60,000 in 1850 to over 170,000 by 1900, driven by coal industry expansion
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining was the dominant industry. Railroads, particularly the Philadelphia & Reading Railroad and the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western, moved coal to market and shaped the settlement pattern of towns.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish and Welsh miners arrived in the 1820s–1870s (earliest wave); German immigrants followed. From the 1880s onward, large influxes of Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians, and Ukrainians arrived, creating a densely layered immigrant community. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian parishes — many ethnically distinct), Welsh Congregational and Baptist, Anglican/Episcopal, Lutheran (German), Methodist, Presbyterian
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (1870s, Schuylkill County); Great Railroad Strike of 1877; Anthracite Coal Strike of 1902; annual mine disasters generating Inspector reports from 1870 onward; formation of the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) in 1890

---

## Boundary changes

- **Lackawanna County (Scranton area) formed from Luzerne County on 13 August 1878.** Any event in the Scranton/Carbondale area before that date was recorded under **Luzerne County** — search Luzerne first for pre-1878 records.
- Schuylkill, Luzerne, Carbon, and Northumberland counties have been stable in their boundaries across the late 1800s research period.
- Carbon County was formed in 1843 from Monroe and Northampton — pre-1843 events in the Carbon area fall under those parent counties.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906**. Philadelphia began city-level registration in 1860; Allegheny County in 1870. No other coal-region county had mandatory civil registration before 1906. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **What this means for 1850–1905:** Births and deaths in coal towns were recorded almost exclusively by churches — civil birth and death records simply do not exist for most families in this region before 1906.
- **Deaths from 1906:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 are fully indexed on FamilySearch (collection [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), 4,218,763 records). Researchers with a subject dying after 1906 — including Patrick Flynn (d. 1908, Schuylkill County) — should search here first.
- **Marriage records (county level):** Marriage licenses and bonds were recorded at the **county courthouse** from the colonial period. FamilySearch holds:
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* ([1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317)) — 524,189 records, indexed + images
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* ([1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)) — 312,045 records, indexed + images
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* ([1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)) — 198,765 records, **index only, no images**
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration exists for the bulk of the target period. Church records are the only substitute (see below).

### Church records

Church records are **the single most important source** for vital events in the coal region before 1906. Ethnic parishes served specific national communities and kept detailed registers in the heritage language of their congregation.

- **Denominations and record types:**
  - *Roman Catholic (Irish):* baptisms, marriages, burials — in Latin or English
  - *Roman Catholic (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian):* separate ethnic parishes from the 1880s onward — registers often in Polish, Lithuanian, or Church Slavonic
  - *Welsh Congregational and Baptist:* baptisms, marriages, burials — in Welsh or English
  - *Lutheran (German):* baptisms, marriages, burials — may be in German through the 1870s
  - *Methodist and Presbyterian:* English-language registers
- **Where held:** Records remain at local parishes, in diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown covers Schuylkill and Carbon; Diocese of Scranton covers Luzerne and Lackawanna), or have been microfilmed by FamilySearch. A synthetic test record appeared in the collections search results labeled as "test fixture" — do not rely on it; contact the diocese and local parishes directly.
- **FamilySearch microfilm:** Many Pennsylvania church registers were filmed; search the FamilySearch catalog by county and denomination for available rolls.
- **Language note:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, and Ukrainian registers require reading those languages. Welsh registers may be in Welsh. German Lutheran registers from before approximately 1880 are commonly in German.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (all indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry). The 1880 census lists all household members with relationship to head. Census schedules list occupation — mining families appear as "miner," "laborer," "mine boss," etc.
- **1890 federal census:** Almost entirely destroyed in a 1921 fire at the Commerce Building in Washington, D.C. A small fragment (Union veterans schedule) survives. This is a significant gap for the coal region.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1885 federal census mortality schedules list individuals who died in the year preceding the census — especially valuable given the frequency of mine accidents and disease in coal towns. Available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **No Pennsylvania state census** was taken during the target period.
- **Tax records as census substitutes:** Pennsylvania county assessment lists (tax duplicates) were taken annually and can substitute for missing census years (see Tax records below).

### Mine and occupational records ⚠️ — unique to coal region

These records are distinctive to the coal mining context and have no equivalent elsewhere:

- **Mine Inspector Reports (1870–):** The Pennsylvania Bureau of Mine Inspection published annual reports from 1870. Each report lists **fatal mine accidents by name, age, nationality, and cause of death** — essentially a vital-record substitute for mining fatalities. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Company employment records:** Colliery companies maintained payrolls, employment cards, and accident reports. These survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties.
  - *Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County, 1870–1900* (FamilySearch vol. 002240015, 410 images): **95% name-indexed + full-text searchable** — the most accessible occupational record online
  - *Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870–1895* (FamilySearch vol. 002240016, 287 images): **browse-only** — must be examined image by image, no name index
  - *Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878–1900* (FamilySearch vol. 002240017, 199 images): **browse-only** — must be examined image by image
  - FamilySearch has 23 total digitized volumes in this category; the 3 above are the first page. 20 additional volumes were not examined — request further pages if needed.
- **UMWA records:** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) maintained membership rolls and grievance files. Contact the UMWA archives for records from the 1890s onward. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Probate and court records

- **Probate:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, and inventories are held at the **county Register of Wills** from county formation onward.
  - FamilySearch: *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* ([1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — 893,214 records, indexed + images
- **Court records:** County Court of Common Pleas handled civil suits, orphans' court, and (pre-1906) naturalizations. Court minute books also record county business — road maintenance assignments, poor-relief payments — naming ordinary residents who appear in no other series.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** — land was distributed by the Penn proprietorship and later the Commonwealth, not the federal government. The Bureau of Land Management GLO website does **not** apply here.
- **Pennsylvania Land Office** (Harrisburg): holds warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681. These are the equivalent of federal-land patents for Pennsylvania families.
- **County deed books:** Held at the **county Recorder of Deeds** from county formation. Mining-community families frequently appear in deed records when they purchased or rented company housing.
- **Tax records (assessment lists/tax duplicates):** Survive from the 1690s in some counties. For the coal region, annual county assessment lists from the mid-1800s onward are held at county archives and historical societies. These serve as the only substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many coal miners served. Spanish-American War (1898).
- **Civil War:** Service records and pension files at NARA (available on Ancestry and Fold3). Pennsylvania regimental records and muster rolls are also at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**. Many coal miners from Irish immigrant families enlisted in Pennsylvania infantry and cavalry regiments.
- **Draft records:** The Civil War draft (Enrollment Act, 1863) generated draft registration lists by county, held at NARA and available on Ancestry/FamilySearch.
- **Pension files** are especially rich — they contain affidavits naming parents, siblings, spouses, and witnesses, making them genealogical gold when vital records are absent.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Coal-region towns have Catholic, Protestant, and non-sectarian cemeteries, often segregated by ethnic community. Church burial registers (see Church records above) are equally important.
- **Online coverage:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com) has broad coverage of Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna county cemeteries. Search by county and town.
- **Mine accident burials:** Mass fatality events (e.g., colliery explosions) sometimes resulted in multiple simultaneous burials in a single churchyard — burial registers from those dates may list several unrelated miners together.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) has been published since 1825 and is the key paper for the coal region — it carried mine accident reports, obituaries, marriage notices, and Molly Maguire trial coverage. Other papers include the *Scranton Republican* (Lackawanna) and the *Wilkes-Barre Record* (Luzerne).
- **Where held:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) (subscription) holds digitized runs of many Pennsylvania papers. The State Library of Pennsylvania (Harrisburg) holds microfilm of the *Miners' Journal* and other regional papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries in coal-region papers frequently name the deceased's place of birth in Ireland, Wales, or Eastern Europe — invaluable for tracing immigrant origins. Accident reports name victims with age and nationality.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary for Irish and German arrivals through the 1870s) and New York/Castle Garden/Ellis Island (primary from the 1880s onward for Eastern European arrivals).
- **Passenger lists:** Available on Ancestry (subscription) and partially on FamilySearch. NARA holds the originals. Post-1895 arrival manifests list last residence and contact person in country of origin — critical for tracing origins.
- **Naturalization records:** Before the Naturalization Act of 1906, any court of record could naturalize — declarations of intention (first papers) and petitions were filed in county Courts of Common Pleas, U.S. District Courts, and other courts. **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.** ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)) After 1906, naturalization was centralized under the Bureau of Naturalization; records are at NARA.
- **Content note:** Post-1906 naturalization petitions ask for birthplace, date of birth, date and port of arrival, and names of witnesses — often neighbors or coworkers from the same mining community.
- **Passenger list manifests** list all passengers including infants and young children traveling with parents — always examine the full manifest page for traveling family members beyond the head of household.

### Tax records

- **Types:** County real-estate and personal property assessment lists (tax duplicates), taken annually.
- **Date range:** Available from county formation; continuous annual runs through the target period.
- **Where held:** County courthouse / county archives and local historical societies. Not consistently digitized.
- **Substitute value:** Tax duplicates are the **primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census** in the coal region — they place a family in a specific township every year.

### Other record types — mutual aid and ethnic organizations

- **Mutual aid societies:** Mining communities supported ethnic fraternal societies (Ancient Order of Hibernians for the Irish; Polish National Alliance; Slovak fraternal orders) that maintained membership records, death benefits, and funeral registers. Contact the relevant national organization archives.
- **Company store records:** Many colliery operators ran company stores; store account books record miner names, purchases, and wages. These survive at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.
- **Published county histories:** Late 19th-century county histories (e.g., *History of Schuylkill County, Pa.*, 1881) contain biographical sketches of long-resident families and transcriptions of early records. Available at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and on Archive.org.

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Administrative centers:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe/Mauch Chunk (Carbon), Sunbury (Northumberland)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominant; railroads (Philadelphia & Reading; Delaware, Lackawanna & Western) shaped town settlement patterns
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish and Welsh (1820s–1870s); German immigrants; then from the 1880s: Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians, Ukrainians
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian — ethnically distinct parishes), Welsh Congregational and Baptist, Lutheran (German), Methodist, Presbyterian

## Boundary changes

- **Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne County, 13 August 1878.** Events in the Scranton/Carbondale area before that date were recorded under Luzerne County.
- Carbon County formed 1843 from Monroe and Northampton — pre-1843 events fall under those parent counties.
- Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Northumberland boundaries were stable across the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Statewide registration began 1906** (births and deaths). No statewide civil birth or death records exist for the coal region before 1906. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- Philadelphia began city-level registration in 1860; Allegheny County in 1870; no coal-region county had mandatory civil registration before 1906.
- **Deaths from 1906:** *Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968* (FamilySearch [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317)) — 4,218,763 records, indexed + images.

- **Gaps:** No birth or death civil registration for 1850–1905. Church records are the only substitute.

### Church records
The single most important source for vital events before 1906.
- **Ethnic parishes:** Irish Catholic (English/Latin registers); Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian Catholic (heritage language); Welsh Congregational/Baptist (Welsh or English); German Lutheran (German through ~1880); Methodist and Presbyterian (English).
- **Where held:** Local parishes, Diocese of Allentown archives (Schuylkill, Carbon), Diocese of Scranton archives (Luzerne, Lackawanna), FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Language note:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian, Welsh, and German registers require reading those languages.

### Census records
- Federal census available: 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (all indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry). Occupation listed as 'miner,' 'laborer,' etc.
- **1890 federal census almost entirely destroyed** (1921 fire). Substitute with county tax duplicates, city directories, and UMWA rolls.
- Mortality schedules 1850–1885 list deaths in the year preceding the census — valuable given mine accident frequency.
- No Pennsylvania state census taken during this period.

### Mine and occupational records (unique to coal region)
- **Mine Inspector annual reports (1870–):** Published annually; list fatal accidents by name, age, nationality, cause of death. At Pennsylvania State Archives. Not digitized online. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

- **Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870–1895** (FamilySearch vol. 002240016, 287 images): **Browse-only** — no name index, must examine image by image.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878–1900** (FamilySearch vol. 002240017, 199 images): **Browse-only** — no name index, must examine image by image.

### Land records
- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state.** BLM GLO website does not apply.
- **Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg):** warrant, survey, and patent records from 1681.
- County deed books at the Recorder of Deeds from county formation. Mining families appear in deeds when purchasing or renting company housing.
- **Tax duplicates (assessment lists):** Annual county records from county formation; primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 census.

### Military records
- Civil War (1861–1865) and Spanish-American War (1898).
- Service records and pension files at NARA (Ancestry, Fold3). Pennsylvania regimental records at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Civil War draft registration lists (1863) at NARA/Ancestry.
- Pension files name parents, siblings, spouses, and witnesses — especially valuable when vital records are absent.

### Cemetery records
- Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon county cemeteries broadly.
- Church burial registers supplement cemetery headstones; mass-fatality accidents may cluster multiple unrelated miners in the same burial register entry.

### Newspaper records
- *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, est. 1825): key coal-region paper. Obituaries frequently name place of birth in Ireland, Wales, or Eastern Europe.
- *Scranton Republican* (Lackawanna), *Wilkes-Barre Record* (Luzerne) also important.
- Newspapers.com (subscription) for digitized runs; State Library of Pennsylvania (Harrisburg) for *Miners' Journal* microfilm.

### Immigration and naturalization records
- **Ports:** Philadelphia (Irish/German arrivals through 1870s); New York/Castle Garden/Ellis Island (Eastern European arrivals from 1880s).

- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** filed in any court of record; Schuylkill County series (1840s–1906) at PA State Archives. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

- Examine full manifest pages — infants and children traveling with parents are listed.

### Tax records
- Annual county assessment lists (tax duplicates) from county formation; held at county archives and historical societies.
- Primary substitute for the destroyed 1890 federal census.
- Not consistently digitized; must be consulted in person or by mail.

### Other records
- **Mutual aid societies:** Ancient Order of Hibernians (Irish), Polish National Alliance, Slovak fraternal orders, Lithuanian Catholic Federation — membership rolls and death-benefit records.
- **Company store ledgers:** Name miners with purchases and wages; at PA State Archives and Historical Society of Schuylkill County.
- **Published county histories:** *History of Schuylkill County, Pa.* (1881) and equivalents contain biographical sketches and transcriptions of early records; many freely available on Archive.org.
